Davy's mischief runs from spoiled preserves and a jug of cream to running off during a Sunday visit, and Anne learns that he behaves better for affection than for punishment. Her own teaching is tested on what she afterwards calls a Jonah day, when nothing goes right, and she finally loses her temper and whips Anthony Pye. She is ashamed of it and apologizes to herself if not to him; oddly, it is from that day that Anthony begins to respect her. The improvement society continues its work, and Anne, Diana, Jane and Priscilla spend a golden day exploring the woods and discovering the neglected garden of Hester Gray, a young wife long dead. Mr. Harrison's household is upset by the arrival of the wife nobody in Avonlea knew he had; she has come to find him after a long separation, and Anne has a hand in reconciling them.

The Harrisons settle down together, Mrs. Harrison cleaning the house thoroughly and banishing Ginger the parrot to the woodshed. Summer brings a run of small calamities and comedies to Green Gables and the school. Paul Irving's stories of his rock people bring Anne up against Mrs. Irving's disapproval of imagination, and Anne defends the boy. Anne and Diana lose their road one afternoon and knock at a stone house up a hidden lane, where they are welcomed by Miss Lavendar Lewis, a small, sweet-faced woman of about forty-five living alone with a little maid called Charlotta the Fourth, keeping herself young by playing at parties for imaginary guests. Anne begins to visit Echo Lodge regularly, and gradually gathers that Miss Lavendar was once engaged to a young man from Avonlea and quarrelled with him over nothing that either could afterwards explain.

Anne takes Paul Irving to Echo Lodge, where he and Miss Lavendar take to one another at once, neither of them knowing what connects them. Anne, piecing together what she has been told, begins to suspect that the man Miss Lavendar refused a quarter of a century ago was Paul's father, and word comes that Stephen Irving is expected back on the Island to see his son. Anne's second year of teaching ends with the school flourishing and even Anthony Pye reconciled to her. Davy has grown into the household and Marilla, who took the twins as a duty, is plainly attached to them. The village improvement society has planted, tidied, and gradually won the older residents round, and the blue hall has been repainted a colour everyone can live with. Anne, who once thought she would go to Redmond, has begun to wonder whether she will ever leave Avonlea at all.

Stephen Irving comes home to Avonlea and goes up the hidden lane to the stone house, and after twenty-five years the quarrel between him and Miss Lavendar is mended; he asks her again and she accepts, with Charlotta the Fourth listening at the door and Paul delighted to be given a mother he already likes. The two are married quietly at Echo Lodge in late August, with Anne and Diana attending. The couple leave for the United States and take Paul and Charlotta with them, so Anne loses her favourite pupil and her friend from the stone house in the same week, though Echo Lodge is to be reopened each summer. At Green Gables the question of Anne's future is answered by a death: Mrs. Rachel Lynde is widowed, and rather than live alone she comes to Green Gables to keep house for Marilla and take charge of the twins. With the household provided for, Marilla insists that Anne go to Redmond College after all. Anne resigns the Avonlea school, and she and Gilbert Blythe leave the village in September for their first term.

characters.description: An eleven-year-old orphan girl sent by mistake to Green Gables, a farm on Prince Edward Island, when the elderly brother and sister who live there had asked for a boy. Thin, freckled, and red-haired, she talks almost without pause, renames the places she loves, and takes refuge in an imagination that turns an ordinary lane into something splendid. She has been passed between households and an asylum since her parents died of fever in her infancy, and has never had a home of her own. She is quick-tempered about her looks, especially her hair, and just as quick to be sorry afterwards.
characters.name: Anne Shirley

characters.description: The shy, elderly bachelor who farms Green Gables with his sister Marilla. He dreads speaking to anyone outside his own household, particularly women, and says very little even at home. He drives to the station to collect the orphan boy the pair had arranged for and finds a talkative red-haired girl waiting instead. Kind by instinct rather than by argument, he is won over almost at once.
characters.name: Matthew Cuthbert

characters.description: Matthew's sister and the mistress of Green Gables, a spare, practical woman of rigid habits and firm opinions who has never had much use for sentiment or for imagination. She intends to send the mistaken orphan straight back. Beneath the sharpness she has a conscience that will not let her hand a child to an unsuitable home, and a dry humour she rarely admits to.
characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert

characters.description: The Cuthberts' nearest neighbour, who sits at her window watching everything that passes on the Avonlea road and considers the affairs of the village her rightful business. Capable, energetic, and famously outspoken, she quilts, runs church societies, and offers her opinion of the new arrival without softening it.
characters.name: Mrs. Rachel Lynde

characters.description: The pretty, black-haired daughter of the Barrys at Orchard Slope, close to Anne in age and the only girl nearby. Good-natured and comfortable rather than imaginative, she becomes the bosom friend Anne has longed for, and the two swear lifelong faithfulness to each other.
characters.name: Diana Barry

characters.description: A clever, good-looking boy at the Avonlea school, older than his classmates because illness kept him out for a time, and much admired by the girls. He teases Anne about her hair on her first day and is astonished by how she takes it.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: The schoolmaster at Avonlea when Anne begins, a young man more interested in courting one of the older pupils than in keeping order, and inclined to punish whoever happens to catch his eye.
characters.name: Mr. Phillips

characters.description: A schoolmate of Anne's, a Pye, and the least friendly of the Avonlea girls: sly, boastful, and fond of setting other children challenges she has no intention of taking up herself.
characters.name: Josie Pye

characters.description: One of Anne's schoolfellows, a fair, plump, giggling girl chiefly interested in her own good looks and in the attention of boys, and a faithful if not very deep friend.
characters.name: Ruby Gillis

characters.description: A sensible, plain-spoken Avonlea girl of Anne's own age, one of the steady friends of her school years, with an eye on teaching as a career.
characters.name: Jane Andrews

characters.description: Diana's mother, a strict and unbending woman who keeps a careful watch over her daughter's company and is not easily persuaded that she has judged a matter wrongly.
characters.name: Mrs. Barry

characters.description: Diana's three-year-old sister, a small child of the Barry household whose sudden illness one winter night brings out an unexpected competence in Anne.
characters.name: Minnie May Barry

characters.description: Diana's wealthy, elderly great-aunt from Charlottetown, a formidable and easily offended lady of decided tastes who is visiting Orchard Slope. She is used to being treated with great care and is unaccustomed to being answered frankly.
characters.name: Miss Josephine Barry

characters.description: The young wife of Avonlea's new minister, warm, cheerful, and genuinely fond of children, who becomes the first grown woman outside Green Gables that Anne takes wholly to heart.
characters.name: Mrs. Allan

characters.description: The new teacher at Avonlea school, a bright, sympathetic young woman who encourages her pupils rather than drilling them, takes them out of doors, and sees what Anne might make of herself with proper study.
characters.name: Miss Muriel Stacy

recaps.ending: Anne finishes her year at Queen's Academy in a single year instead of two, wins the Avery scholarship for English, and comes home to Green Gables expecting to go on to Redmond College in the autumn. Gilbert Blythe takes the gold medal. That summer Matthew, whose heart has been failing, dies suddenly after learning that the bank holding the Cuthberts' savings has failed. Marilla is left alone with a farm she cannot work and eyes that are failing her; the doctor warns that she will lose her sight altogether unless she gives up close work and worry, and she speaks of selling Green Gables. Anne gives up the scholarship and Redmond, arranges to board at home, and takes a teaching post so that she and Marilla can keep the farm. When she finds that the Avonlea school has been promised to her, she learns that Gilbert has withdrawn his own application and taken the school at White Sands so that she could stay near Marilla. Meeting him at the gate, Anne finally puts an end to the quarrel she has kept up for five years, and the two part as friends with plans to study together. Anne sets out on a narrower road than the one she had imagined, and finds she is content with it.
recaps.in_short: Elderly brother and sister Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert of Green Gables, on Prince Edward Island, send for an orphan boy to help on the farm and are sent eleven-year-old Anne Shirley instead. Marilla means to return her, but relents, and the talkative, imaginative, red-haired child stays. Anne makes a bosom friend of Diana Barry, begins a five-year feud with Gilbert Blythe after he teases her about her hair, and stumbles through a series of scrapes: an accidental dose of currant wine, a dyed-green head, a broken ankle on a dare. She also grows into the village's affection, saving Diana's little sister from croup and winning over her sternest critics. Marilla, who cannot say what she feels, comes to love her; Matthew, who never could say anything, quietly always did. Anne takes the entrance examinations for Queen's Academy, ties with Gilbert for first place, and wins a scholarship. Then Matthew dies and Marilla's sight begins to fail. Anne gives up the scholarship, takes a country school, and stays at Green Gables, making peace with Gilbert at last.

recaps.text: Mrs. Rachel Lynde, who misses nothing that happens on the Avonlea road, is astonished to see her neighbour Matthew Cuthbert drive off in his good clothes on a weekday, and learns from Marilla that the elderly brother and sister have arranged to adopt an orphan boy to help with the farm work at Green Gables. At Bright River station Matthew finds no boy, but a thin, red-haired girl of about eleven sitting on a pile of shingles, entirely certain that she is the one he has come for. She talks the whole way home about the countryside, renaming the places she likes best, and Matthew, who is too shy to explain, cannot bring himself to tell her there has been a mistake. Marilla says flatly that they wanted a boy, and the child is heartbroken. She is put to bed in the east gable, and Marilla determines to return her to the orphan asylum and find out how the error was made.

Anne tells the Cuthberts her history: both parents dead of fever when she was a baby, then years of minding other people's children before the asylum. Marilla drives her to see Mrs. Spencer, who arranged the mix-up, and finds that a hard, worn woman named Mrs. Blewett wants the girl as a drudge. Marilla cannot hand a child over to that, and after a struggle with her own reluctance she decides to keep Anne. Anne's education in Cuthbert respectability begins at once: prayers, catechism, and a hat trimmed with flowers that shocks the congregation. When Mrs. Rachel Lynde calls and remarks on Anne's thinness, freckles, and red hair, Anne turns on her furiously. Marilla insists on an apology; Anne refuses, is confined to her room, then delivers an apology so dramatically penitent that Mrs. Rachel forgives her outright and privately admits she took a liking to the child.

Anne meets Diana Barry of Orchard Slope and the two swear eternal friendship, giving Anne the bosom friend she has always wanted. She joins the Avonlea school, where the master, Mr. Phillips, keeps poor order. On her first day Gilbert Blythe tries to get her attention by calling her Carrots; Anne breaks her slate over his head and swears never to speak to him again, and when she is punished for a lateness that was not her fault she refuses to return to school until she chooses to. Earlier, wanting badly to attend a Sunday-school picnic, she confesses to losing Marilla's amethyst brooch, a confession she invented, only for the brooch to be found caught on Marilla's shawl. Invited to entertain Diana alone, Anne serves her what she believes is raspberry cordial; it is currant wine, Diana goes home unsteady and ill, and Mrs. Barry forbids the friendship, which Anne takes as the ruin of her life.

One winter night Diana runs for Anne because her little sister Minnie May is choking with croup and the parents are away. Anne, who has nursed croupy children before, works over her until the doctor arrives; Mrs. Barry, told that Anne saved the child, apologizes and restores the friendship. Anne's scrapes continue. Staying overnight after a concert, she and Diana leap into a spare-room bed in the dark and land on Diana's formidable great-aunt Josephine, who is so charmed by Anne's honest explanation that she becomes her friend. Anne frightens herself out of the spruce wood she has filled with imaginary ghosts, flavours a cake with liniment for the new minister's wife, Mrs. Allan, and is forgiven. Then, dared by Josie Pye at a party, she walks the ridgepole of a kitchen roof, falls, and breaks her ankle, spending seven weeks laid up and visited by half of Avonlea.

A new teacher, Miss Stacy, comes to Avonlea and transforms the school, taking her pupils out of doors and putting the older ones through preparation for the Queen's Academy entrance examinations. Anne rehearses for a Christmas concert, and Matthew, noticing that her sleeves are not like the other girls', secretly arranges with Mrs. Rachel Lynde for a dress with puffed sleeves. Anne and her friends form a story club. Vanity brings its own punishment: a pedlar sells Anne a dye promised to turn her hair a raven black, it turns green instead, and the hair has to be cut off. Playing the drowned Elaine in a flat-bottomed dory, Anne is left clinging to a bridge pile when the boat leaks and sinks, and is rescued by Gilbert Blythe, whose offer of friendship she refuses on the spot and privately regrets. In the autumn she visits Miss Barry in Charlottetown for the Exhibition.

Miss Stacy forms a Queen's class of the older pupils, and Anne studies for it with a will, chiefly because Gilbert Blythe is in it and she means not to be beaten. Diana, who is not preparing for the examinations, is left out, and the two friends feel the first change in their lives. Anne is fifteen and growing tall and quiet; Marilla, watching her, admits to herself how much the house would lack without her. In June the whole class travels to Charlottetown for the entrance examinations, and Anne waits in an agony of suspense until the pass list is printed: she and Gilbert are tied for first place out of the whole Island. Matthew and Marilla are openly proud. That summer Anne recites at a concert in the White Sands hotel among wealthy guests, comes home to Green Gables, and tells Diana she would rather be herself in Avonlea than any of them.

Anne boards in Charlottetown for the Queen's year, homesick at first, then absorbed in work, and takes the two-year course in one. At the close she wins the Avery scholarship in English, which would pay for four years at Redmond College; Gilbert takes the gold medal. She comes home to a joyful Green Gables, but Matthew looks ill and Marilla admits her eyes are failing. Days later Matthew collapses and dies of heart failure after reading that the bank holding the Cuthberts' money has failed. Marilla, grieving and half blind, says she will have to sell Green Gables, since she cannot manage the farm alone. Anne gives up the scholarship and her place at Redmond, arranges to teach and board at home, and refuses to be argued out of it. When the Avonlea school is offered to her she learns that Gilbert has stepped aside and taken White Sands instead so that she could stay with Marilla. Anne stops him at the gate and ends the long quarrel; they part as friends, and she looks at the narrowed road ahead of her without regret.

characters.description: An observant, talkative eleven-year-old orphan sent from an asylum to Green Gables by mistake. Anne longs for a home and family, invents romantic names for ordinary places, and is acutely sensitive about her red hair and thin appearance. Her imagination and impulsiveness make her arrival disruptive, while her eagerness to love Avonlea quickly becomes clear.
characters.name: Anne Shirley

characters.description: The reserved, painfully shy brother of Marilla Cuthbert. He works the Green Gables farm and finds social encounters difficult, especially with women and girls. Sent to collect the boy he and Marilla expect to adopt, he instead meets Anne and is quietly won over by her conversation during the drive home.
characters.name: Matthew Cuthbert

characters.description: Matthew's unmarried sister and the practical manager of Green Gables. Exacting, restrained, and accustomed to an orderly life, she has agreed to adopt a boy who can help on the farm. The arrival of an imaginative girl instead confronts her with a decision she had not prepared to make.
characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert

characters.description: The Cuthberts' outspoken neighbor, known throughout Avonlea for combining energetic community work with close attention to everyone else's affairs. She notices Matthew's unusual trip away from the farm and immediately sets out to learn its purpose.
characters.name: Mrs. Rachel Lynde

characters.description: A girl of Anne's age who lives near Green Gables. Pretty, warm, and more conventionally brought up than Anne, she agrees to become Anne's closest friend in a solemn ceremony beside the Barry garden.
characters.name: Diana Barry

characters.description: A handsome, confident Avonlea schoolboy returning after time away. He tries to attract the new girl's attention by teasing her about her red hair, provoking an angry response and beginning a determined rivalry.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: The teacher at Avonlea school when Anne first attends. Young and self-important, he pays conspicuous attention to an older pupil and handles classroom discipline in ways that can humiliate his students.
characters.name: Mr. Phillips

characters.description: Diana's strict, socially conscious mother. She permits Diana's friendship with Anne but expects both girls to behave properly and judges Anne by the mishaps that occur in her home.
characters.name: Mrs. Barry

characters.description: Diana's much younger sister. When she becomes dangerously ill with croup while the adults are away, Anne draws on experience gained while caring for children in an earlier household.
characters.name: Minnie May Barry

characters.description: Diana's wealthy elderly great-aunt, visiting the Barry household from Charlottetown. She is sharp-tongued and formidable, and her unexpected presence turns one of Anne and Diana's indoor adventures into a serious social offense.
characters.name: Aunt Josephine Barry

characters.description: A fashionable, energetic young teacher who takes charge of the Avonlea school. She encourages her pupils through special projects and ambitious study, giving Anne a model of education founded on sympathy as well as discipline.
characters.name: Miss Stacy

characters.description: One of Anne's Avonlea classmates and a member of the socially prominent Pye family. Critical and competitive, she frequently irritates Anne and represents a rival within the girls' school circle.
characters.name: Josie Pye

characters.description: A friendly, romantic Avonlea schoolgirl in Anne and Diana's circle. She is especially interested in stories of love and courtship and later joins the group preparing for the Queen's Academy entrance examinations.
characters.name: Ruby Gillis

characters.description: A sensible Avonlea classmate who becomes part of Anne's close school circle. She shares the girls' games and, as they grow older, studies alongside Anne for the Queen's Academy entrance examinations.
characters.name: Jane Andrews

recaps.ending: Matthew dies suddenly after learning that the bank holding the Cuthberts' savings has failed. Soon afterward Marilla's worsening eyesight threatens to force her to sell Green Gables, because she cannot manage the farm alone. Anne, who has won the Avery Scholarship and planned to continue her education at Redmond College, gives up the scholarship so she can remain with Marilla and teach nearby. Gilbert has been appointed to the Avonlea school, but he quietly gives up the post so Anne can take it and accepts a more distant school himself. His generosity ends their long estrangement, and Anne finally offers the friendship he has wanted. Green Gables is preserved, Marilla is no longer alone, and Anne faces a smaller life than she expected but sees it as a beginning rather than a defeat.
recaps.in_short: Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert intend to adopt a boy to help at Green Gables, but a mistake sends them Anne Shirley, an imaginative red-haired orphan. Matthew immediately cares for her; Marilla gradually decides to keep her and grows to love her. Anne's temper and romantic ideas cause repeated disasters, yet she finds a devoted friend in Diana Barry, proves resourceful in a crisis, and wins a place in Avonlea's community. She treats Gilbert Blythe as an enemy after he mocks her hair, and their academic rivalry drives both toward Queen's Academy. Anne earns the Avery Scholarship, but Matthew dies and Marilla's failing eyesight endangers Green Gables. Anne gives up further study to stay home and teach. Gilbert surrenders the Avonlea school for her benefit, and she finally reconciles with him, accepting an altered future rooted in the home she once feared she would lose.

recaps.text: Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert, unmarried siblings who live at Green Gables in Avonlea, decide to adopt an orphan boy who can help Matthew with farm work. Through a misunderstanding, eleven-year-old Anne Shirley is waiting at the station instead. Matthew, shy and gentle, is quickly charmed during the drive home by her nonstop conversation and delight in the landscape. Practical Marilla insists that the error must be corrected, devastating Anne, who has already begun to imagine Green Gables as her home. Anne explains that she has spent her childhood moving between difficult households and an orphan asylum, with little affection or security. When Marilla takes her to Mrs. Spencer to resolve the mistake, another woman offers to take Anne chiefly as unpaid help with children. Marilla recoils from that prospect and realizes she is unwilling to surrender the girl. She brings Anne back to Green Gables and decides to keep her on trial, while making clear that the lively child will require careful upbringing.

Anne begins learning the routines and expectations of Green Gables. Her unconventional prayer, elaborate imagination, and strong emotions repeatedly test Marilla's patience, but they also reveal how unfamiliar she is with being cared for. When outspoken neighbor Rachel Lynde criticizes Anne's appearance, Anne furiously insults her. Marilla requires an apology; Anne eventually delivers an extravagant one that satisfies Rachel and restores peace. Matthew remains Anne's quiet ally, while Marilla's stern guidance increasingly carries genuine concern. Anne attends church and Sunday school, though she is more interested in the flowers on her hat and in imaginative possibilities than in the dull lessons. Her greatest wish is to have a close friend. Marilla arranges for her to meet Diana Barry, the girl living across the pond. Anne and Diana immediately pledge lasting friendship, and Anne begins to feel that Avonlea can give her both the belonging and companionship she has long wanted.

Anne's delight in Avonlea is repeatedly interrupted by impulsive mistakes. After Marilla's brooch disappears, Anne invents a confession so she will be allowed to attend a picnic, only for the brooch to be found where Marilla left it. At school Gilbert Blythe teases Anne about her red hair. She breaks her slate over his head and refuses his apology, beginning a rivalry that continues even when their teacher punishes her unfairly. During a tea party Anne accidentally serves Diana currant wine instead of raspberry cordial. Mrs. Barry assumes Anne deliberately made Diana drunk and forbids the friendship. The separation leaves both girls miserable. Anne later faces an emergency when Diana's little sister Minnie May develops croup while the adults are away. Drawing on her earlier experience caring for children, Anne directs the treatment that keeps Minnie May alive until the doctor arrives. A grateful Mrs. Barry acknowledges Anne's competence and allows her friendship with Diana to resume.

Anne and Diana's midnight attempt to frighten a friend goes wrong when they leap onto a bed occupied by Diana's formidable Aunt Josephine. Anne's sincere apology and lively personality eventually win the older woman over, and the girls gain an unexpected friend. Anne continues to turn romantic ideas into mishaps: while acting out a story, she is stranded in a leaking boat and must accept rescue from Gilbert, yet she still rejects his attempt at reconciliation. Other disasters include flavoring a cake with liniment and falling from a roof after accepting a dare. Beneath the accidents, Anne is becoming more secure and capable. A new teacher, Miss Stacy, encourages the pupils with nature studies, exercises, and plans for a school concert. Matthew, recognizing how different Anne looks from the other girls, insists that she receive a fashionable dress with puffed sleeves. The successful Christmas concert and Matthew's gift confirm that Anne is no longer merely a trial resident at Green Gables but a cherished member of the household and community.

Anne's adventures gradually give way to adolescence and disciplined ambition. Attempts to dye her hated red hair leave it green and force a severe haircut; a reenactment of an Arthurian scene leaves her boat sinking. Miss Stacy organizes an advanced class to prepare selected pupils for the Queen's Academy entrance examination. Anne studies intensely alongside Diana, Jane, Ruby, Josie, and Gilbert. Her rivalry with Gilbert becomes quieter but remains a powerful motivation, even as she begins to understand that her old anger has isolated her from someone she respects. The passing seasons bring physical and emotional change, and Marilla feels both pride and sorrow as the talkative child matures. Anne and Gilbert tie for first place in the entrance results. At a hotel concert, Anne initially feels out of place among fashionable visitors, but her recitation wins the audience. She then leaves Avonlea for Queen's Academy, where she misses Green Gables while working through the compressed teacher-training course and competing with Gilbert for academic honors.

At Queen's Academy, Gilbert wins the gold medal while Anne receives the Avery Scholarship, which would fund further study at Redmond College. She returns to Green Gables full of plans, but family circumstances overturn them. The Abbey Bank fails, wiping out Matthew and Marilla's savings, and the shock contributes to Matthew's sudden death. Anne and Marilla grieve together, their restraint giving way to a more openly expressed love. Marilla then reveals that her eyesight is failing and that she may have to sell Green Gables because she cannot run it alone. Anne gives up the scholarship and chooses to remain home, planning to teach locally and continue studying independently. Gilbert, who had secured the Avonlea school, gives it up so Anne can take the post and accepts another assignment farther away. Anne thanks him, ends their long quarrel, and agrees that they can be friends. Her future has narrowed from her earlier plans, but Green Gables will remain their home, and she meets the changed path with hope.

characters.description: An unmarried farmer at Green Gables, shy with women and more comfortable with quiet routines. Matthew agrees that he and his sister need a boy to help on the farm, but his gentle sympathy quickly makes him receptive to the unexpected child waiting at the station.
characters.name: Matthew Cuthbert

characters.description: Matthew's practical, plain-spoken sister and co-owner of Green Gables. Marilla has arranged to adopt an orphan boy for farm help and is dismayed by the mistake that brings Anne, though her strong sense of duty requires that the girl's future be settled responsibly.
characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert

characters.description: The Cuthberts' outspoken neighbor, known for observing Avonlea's affairs and giving her opinion without invitation. Mrs Lynde is industrious and generally well intentioned, but her blunt judgments can be painful.
characters.name: Rachel Lynde

characters.description: An eleven-year-old orphan mistakenly sent to the Cuthberts instead of the boy they requested. Anne is thin, red-haired, intensely talkative, and gifted with an imagination that transforms ordinary places into romantic landscapes. Years of unstable care have made her hungry for affection and for a permanent home.
characters.name: Anne Shirley

characters.description: The woman who collected Anne from the orphan asylum while arranging a boy for the Cuthberts. Mrs Spencer's misunderstanding has brought Anne to Green Gables, and she offers to reverse the mistake when Marilla questions the arrangement.
characters.name: Mrs Spencer

characters.description: A girl of Anne's age who lives near Green Gables. Warm, loyal, and more conventionally brought up than Anne, Diana readily accepts Anne's solemn proposal that they become devoted lifelong friends.
characters.name: Diana Barry

characters.description: Diana's strict and socially proper mother. Mrs Barry permits Anne and Diana's friendship but expects good behavior and is quick to withdraw her trust when she believes Anne has acted irresponsibly.
characters.name: Mrs Barry

characters.description: A clever, confident Avonlea schoolboy who has been away when Anne first joins the class. Accustomed to being popular and to competing for first place, Gilbert tries to attract the new girl's attention with teasing about her red hair.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: The Avonlea teacher when Anne begins school. Mr Phillips is vain and inconsistent, and his careless handling of discipline intensifies Anne's embarrassment rather than earning her respect.
characters.name: Mr Phillips

characters.description: Diana's younger sister. Minnie May becomes dangerously ill with croup while the adults are away, leaving Anne to draw on practical knowledge learned during her years caring for other families' children.
characters.name: Minnie May Barry

characters.description: Diana's elderly, wealthy great-aunt from Charlottetown. Initially severe after Anne and Diana accidentally disturb her, she proves receptive to Anne's apology and amused by the girl's honesty and imagination.
characters.name: Josephine Barry

characters.description: The energetic new teacher at Avonlea school. Miss Stacy introduces outdoor lessons, compositions, recitations, and serious preparation for higher study, giving Anne an admired adult example and a demanding academic goal.
characters.name: Miss Stacy

recaps.ending: Anne completes her year at Queen's Academy, ties with Gilbert for first-class honors, and wins the Avery scholarship, which would allow her to attend college. Her plans change after Matthew dies suddenly and Marilla learns that her eyesight may fail if she continues working too hard. Anne decides to remain at Green Gables and teach nearby so Marilla will not have to sell their home. Gilbert has already received the Avonlea school but gives it up for Anne, accepting a more distant post himself. His generosity ends their long estrangement, and they finally agree to be friends. Anne's future is narrower than the ambitious route she had expected, yet she regards it as purposeful rather than defeated: Green Gables is secure for the present, Marilla will have her support, and education and writing remain open to her in new forms.
recaps.in_short: Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert intend to adopt a boy to help at Green Gables but receive imaginative, red-haired Anne Shirley instead. Marilla keeps her after learning how precarious the orphan's alternatives are, and Anne gradually becomes central to both Cuthberts' lives. Her impulsiveness causes comic disasters, while her loyalty, courage, and eagerness to learn win over Avonlea. She forms a deep friendship with Diana Barry and a fierce academic rivalry with Gilbert Blythe after he mocks her hair. Guided by the progressive teacher Miss Stacy, Anne earns a place at Queen's Academy and wins a scholarship. Matthew then dies, and Marilla's failing eyesight threatens the loss of Green Gables. Anne gives up immediate college plans to remain with Marilla and teach locally. Gilbert surrenders the Avonlea post so she can stay near home; Anne forgives him, and their rivalry becomes friendship as she accepts a changed but still hopeful future.

recaps.text: Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, unmarried siblings who farm at Green Gables in Avonlea, arrange to adopt an orphan boy who can help Matthew. A misunderstanding sends eleven-year-old Anne Shirley instead. Matthew finds the talkative, imaginative child immediately appealing, while practical Marilla insists the mistake must be corrected. Anne's delight in the landscape and desperate hope of belonging make the prospect of being sent away painful. When Marilla investigates, she learns that Anne's childhood has consisted of bereavement, unpaid work in troubled households, and an orphan asylum. Another woman is willing to take Anne mainly as a caretaker for several children. Marilla refuses to leave her to that fate and decides on a trial at Green Gables, though she makes clear that Anne must learn obedience and self-control.

Anne begins adjusting to Green Gables. She struggles with formal prayers and ordinary chores but responds eagerly when Marilla offers firm, fair guidance. Mrs Rachel Lynde insults Anne's appearance, and Anne answers with an explosive denunciation. Marilla requires an apology; Anne eventually delivers an elaborate one, and Mrs Lynde accepts it. Marilla also discovers that Anne did not steal a missing brooch after all: Anne had invented a confession because she thought it was the only way to be allowed on a picnic, while the brooch had simply fallen behind furniture. The incident forces Marilla to recognize the danger of judging the child too quickly. Anne attends the church picnic, tastes ice cream, and gains confidence that Green Gables may truly become her home.

Anne meets Diana Barry and the girls declare themselves inseparable friends. At school Anne joins the social and academic life of Avonlea, but Gilbert Blythe teases her about her red hair. Furious, she breaks her slate over his head and refuses his apology. The teacher, Mr Phillips, humiliates her further by making her sit beside Gilbert, so Anne temporarily leaves school and studies at home. A tea party for Diana creates another disaster when Anne accidentally serves currant wine instead of raspberry cordial. Diana becomes drunk, and Mrs Barry forbids the friendship despite Anne's truthful explanation. The loss is devastating to Anne, while Marilla sees more clearly how deeply the child now cares about people and place.

Anne's experience caring for younger children becomes unexpectedly useful when Diana's little sister Minnie May develops a dangerous case of croup while the adults are absent. Anne treats her calmly until the doctor arrives, saving the child's life and restoring Mrs Barry's trust. Anne and Diana resume their friendship. Later they accidentally jump onto the bed where Diana's visiting Aunt Josephine is sleeping, but Anne's sincere apology wins the older woman over. Anne's imagination continues to create trouble: after filling familiar woods with invented ghosts, she terrifies herself on an evening errand. In a more serious accident, she accepts a dare to walk along a roof ridge, falls, and breaks her ankle. During her recovery she remains surrounded by friends, evidence that she now belongs to a community.

Miss Stacy becomes Avonlea's teacher and transforms school through nature study, composition, performances, and ambitious lessons. Anne flourishes under her encouragement. A cooking attempt goes wrong when Anne unknowingly flavors a cake with medicine, but the visiting minister's wife treats the mistake kindly. At a concert Anne gives a successful recitation and begins to see that her dramatic gifts can be disciplined rather than merely impulsive. A boating game based on a romantic poem nearly ends in disaster when Anne's leaky boat sinks and she is stranded beneath a bridge. Gilbert rescues her and again asks for friendship, but Anne's pride keeps her from accepting. She later realizes that her refusal has cost her something, though their academic rivalry continues.

As Anne grows older, her ambitions become more focused. Miss Stacy forms a special class to prepare promising pupils for the entrance examination to Queen's Academy. Anne studies intensely alongside Diana, Jane, Ruby, and others, with Gilbert as her closest rival. A visit to Charlottetown and an appearance at a hotel concert expose her to a wider social world; although intimidated by a professional performer, Anne discovers that honest feeling can matter more than polish. She passes the Queen's entrance examination, tied with Gilbert at the top, and prepares to leave Avonlea for a year of advanced study. The change brings pride and sadness: Diana will remain at home, while Anne's bond with Matthew and Marilla has become that of a daughter leaving her parents.

At Queen's Academy, Anne compresses a two-year course into one and competes with Gilbert for honors. She wins the Avery scholarship, opening a path to college, while Gilbert earns a teaching qualification. Returning to Green Gables, Anne looks forward to further study, but Matthew dies suddenly after learning that the bank holding the family's savings has failed. Marilla then reveals that her eyesight is deteriorating and that she may have to sell Green Gables. Anne gives up the scholarship and chooses to teach locally while studying independently, allowing her to remain with Marilla. Gilbert, who had secured the Avonlea school, quietly takes another position so Anne can teach close to home. His sacrifice finally ends her resentment; they become friends. Anne accepts that her immediate horizon has changed, but she faces it with hope and a secure sense of belonging.

characters.description: Mistress of Ingleside, the big house at Glen St. Mary, and the mother of a growing family. She is in her thirties, busy with a country doctor's household, and still the woman who names places and takes an interest in everyone's affairs, though her days now belong to her children. The book opens with a short visit back to Avonlea, and returns her to a house where she is needed at every hour.
characters.name: Anne Blythe

characters.description: The doctor at Glen St. Mary, with a large country practice that keeps him out at all hours and absorbed in difficult cases. Devoted to Anne and to his children, he is not always quick to notice what is going on in his own house.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: The Blythes' housekeeper and the real power in the Ingleside kitchen, fiercely loyal to the family, sharp-tongued about outsiders, and convinced that no children anywhere are the equals of these. She keeps a private opinion of everyone in the Glen and shares most of them.
characters.name: Susan Baker

characters.description: The eldest Blythe child, a sturdy, adventurous boy full of plans and enthusiasms, devoted to his dog and to whatever scheme is in hand, and the ringleader of the younger ones.
characters.name: Jem Blythe

characters.description: The second Blythe son, a beautiful, dreamy boy who loves words and makes poems in his head. He feels everything more sharply than his brothers and sisters, is frightened by ugliness and cruelty, and is teased for it by children who do not understand him.
characters.name: Walter Blythe

characters.description: One of the Blythe twins, a serious, imaginative girl with brown eyes who takes her own daydreams very seriously and can persuade herself of almost anything.
characters.name: Nan Blythe

characters.description: Nan's twin, red-haired like her mother and more headstrong, given to violent friendships with unsuitable girls and to defending them past all reason.
characters.name: Di Blythe

characters.description: The quiet Blythe son, brown-haired and self-contained, Susan's particular favourite since she nursed him through a difficult infancy, and the child who gives the least trouble.
characters.name: Shirley Blythe

characters.description: The youngest Blythe, a baby daughter born at Ingleside and named for Anne's own mother and for Marilla Cuthbert. She grows through the book from an infant into a small, vain, lisping girl who takes everything to heart.
characters.name: Bertha Marilla Blythe

characters.description: An elderly aunt of Gilbert's who arrives at Ingleside for a short visit. Mournful, faultfinding, and impossible to please, she disapproves of the children's upbringing, the household's meals, and Anne's management, and delivers her judgements with an air of wounded duty.
characters.name: Aunt Mary Maria Blythe

characters.description: Formerly Miss Cornelia Bryant of Four Winds, now married and living at the Glen, still the sharpest tongue and the kindest hand in the district, and still ready to explain to Anne exactly what is wrong with everybody.
characters.name: Mrs. Marshall Elliott

characters.description: The mistress of Green Gables, very old now, whom Anne visits in Avonlea at the opening of the book, and who is still the fixed point of Anne's childhood.
characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert

characters.description: Anne's bosom friend of childhood, now Mrs. Fred Wright and the mother of a family of her own, with whom Anne spends a few days of remembering at the opening of the book.
characters.name: Diana Wright

characters.description: A schoolfellow of Di Blythe's from a poor and disorderly family, a fluent and inventive liar who dazzles Di with impossible accounts of her relations and her home.
characters.name: Jenny Penny

characters.description: Another of Di Blythe's brief and unsuitable friendships, a girl who wins Di's sympathy with a tale of being ill-used at home and enjoys the attention it brings her.
characters.name: Delilah Green

characters.description: A woman Gilbert knew at college, now handsome, prosperous, and rather self-satisfied, who reappears in the Blythes' social circle and unsettles Anne more than she likes to admit.
characters.name: Christine Stuart

recaps.ending: Anne's fear that Gilbert has stopped loving her comes to a head when they attend a dinner in town where Christine Stuart, an old acquaintance of his college days, is among the guests. Anne dresses carefully and spends the evening watching the two of them, wretched with an unhappiness she has never felt before. On the drive home Gilbert speaks of Christine with amused indifference, remarking on how much she has changed and how glad he is to be going home, and the whole structure of Anne's jealousy collapses. His distraction, it turns out, was nothing but overwork and worry over a difficult case. The two are entirely at ease with each other again. Aunt Mary Maria has long since taken herself off, and Ingleside is its own household once more. Each of the children's troubles has been survived and mostly outgrown: Jem is full of plans, Walter is writing, the twins have finished with their unsuitable friendships, and Rilla is out of babyhood. The book ends on a quiet summer night at Ingleside with the whole family asleep under one roof and Anne content, the family established for the books that follow.
recaps.in_short: Anne Blythe is settled at Ingleside, the doctor's house at Glen St. Mary, with Gilbert's country practice, the redoubtable housekeeper Susan Baker, and a family of children: Jem, Walter, the twins Nan and Di, Shirley, and, born in this book, the youngest, Rilla. The story is a sequence of domestic episodes rather than a single plot. Gilbert's Aunt Mary Maria arrives for a short visit and stays for months, spreading gloom and criticism until she takes offence and leaves of her own accord, to the household's relief. Each child has a chapter of their own troubles: Jem loses his dog, Walter is frightened into walking home alone in the night by a story that his mother is dying, Nan convinces herself she was exchanged in infancy and goes to find her supposed real mother, and Di is twice taken in by a friend who lies to her. Anne, turning forty, begins to fear that Gilbert has grown indifferent to her, a fear that a dinner party attended by an old acquaintance of his makes almost unbearable, until his own words on the way home show it to be groundless.

recaps.text: Previously: Anne Shirley grew up as an orphan taken in at Green Gables in Avonlea, taught school, took her degree at Redmond College, and married Gilbert Blythe after a long engagement. They began married life in a small house on Four Winds Harbour, where Anne's first baby died within a day of birth, where she made friends of the old lighthouse keeper Captain Jim, the outspoken Miss Cornelia Bryant, and Leslie Moore, and where her son Jem was born. Captain Jim died, Leslie was freed from a marriage that had never legally existed and married the writer Owen Ford, Miss Cornelia married Marshall Elliott, and the Blythes moved up to a larger house at Glen St. Mary called Ingleside, taking with them their housekeeper Susan Baker. Several years have passed since then; Gilbert's practice has grown, and the Ingleside nursery has filled. This book is a series of scenes from the family's life in those years.

Anne is in Avonlea for a few days, staying at Green Gables and talking over old times with Diana, now Mrs. Fred Wright. The two walk their childhood haunts, remember the friends of their schooldays and what has become of them, and Anne goes home to Glen St. Mary. Ingleside is full: Gilbert out at all hours on his practice, Susan Baker ruling the kitchen and the family's reputation, and the children, Jem, Walter, the twins Nan and Di, and small Shirley, filling the house and grounds. Anne's sixth child, a daughter, is born and named Bertha Marilla after Anne's own mother and Marilla Cuthbert, and is called Rilla from the start. Susan is triumphant. Neighbours call, chiefly Mrs. Marshall Elliott, once Miss Cornelia Bryant of Four Winds, who brings the Glen's news and her verdict on it, and the household settles into the ordinary business of a doctor's family in a small country place.

Gilbert's elderly aunt, Mary Maria Blythe, comes to Ingleside for what is announced as a short visit and settles in with no sign of leaving. She is mournful and endlessly critical: the children are ill brought up, the meals are wrong, Anne's management is careless, and every remark carries the suggestion that she is being badly used. Susan Baker, whose kitchen is invaded, endures her with visible effort, and Gilbert, who cannot be brought to see the trouble, treats his aunt as a harmless old lady. The children learn to keep out of her way. Meanwhile the ordinary griefs of childhood arrive at Ingleside: Jem's dog sickens and dies, and Jem grieves for him with the whole of his heart. Anne's household runs on under the strain, and the visit stretches from weeks into months.

Walter, the dreaming, sensitive Blythe boy, is sent away to stay with relatives at Lowbridge. He is miserable there, and an older girl, half in mischief and half in cruelty, tells him that his mother is dying and that he will never see her again. Believing it, he sets out at night and walks the long road home alone, terrified the whole way, and arrives at Ingleside to find his mother perfectly well and the house calm. The incident marks him; he has more imagination than he can always control, and the world outside Ingleside frightens him. Other episodes fill the season, small quarrels, schemes, and reconciliations among the children, while Aunt Mary Maria remains and the family's patience wears thinner with every week she stays.

Aunt Mary Maria's presence has become intolerable. She interferes in the nursery, offends the neighbours, and turns every kindness into a grievance, and Anne, who will not be rude to a guest under her own roof, is worn down by it. Susan is close to open rebellion. Matters end not in a quarrel but in an accident of manners: a party is planned in the old lady's honour, something at it strikes her as a slight, and she announces with dignity that she has stayed where she was not wanted and will trouble them no longer. She departs, and Ingleside becomes itself again overnight. The relief in the household is enormous and largely unspoken. Anne turns back to her children, her garden, and the affairs of the Glen.

The children's own troubles occupy the following seasons. Nan, who takes her fancies seriously, works herself into the conviction that she was exchanged for another baby at birth, and goes secretly to the poor household where she believes her real mother lives; the visit cures her of the idea entirely and sends her home grateful for what she has. Di attaches herself twice over to unsuitable friends: one a fluent liar from a disorderly farm whose invented family history collapses when Di spends a night under her roof, the other a girl who wins her sympathy with a tale of ill-usage and enjoys the fuss. Both friendships end in disillusionment and no lasting harm. Jem's ambitions grow, Walter goes on writing his verses, and Shirley and Rilla are still small. Anne watches them all with a mother's mixture of amusement and anxiety.

Anne, now forty, is troubled by a fear she cannot shake off: Gilbert is preoccupied, absent-minded, and short with her, forgets what matters to her, and seems to have stopped noticing that she exists. She persuades herself that his love has worn out and that she has grown old and dull. The fear reaches its worst when they go to a dinner in town where Christine Stuart, whom Gilbert knew at Redmond and whom Anne once believed he might marry, is among the guests. Anne spends the evening watching them together and is thoroughly wretched. On the drive home Gilbert speaks of Christine with complete indifference, says how much she has aged and how glad he is to be going home, and the whole of Anne's misery falls away; his distraction had been nothing but overwork and a case he could not save. The book closes on a warm summer night at Ingleside with the household asleep, the children safe, and Anne entirely happy.

characters.description: Eighteen and about to leave Avonlea for Redmond College in Kingsport, on the mainland, after two years of teaching. She has kept the imagination and the ready tongue of her childhood and gained a good deal of self-possession, and she is aware that going away will change the village and her friendships in ways she cannot prevent. She writes stories, means to take her degree, and holds firm romantic notions about what love ought to feel like when it comes.
characters.name: Anne Shirley

characters.description: Anne's old schoolfellow and rival, now bound for Redmond himself, where he intends to work towards medicine. Steady, hard-working, and popular, he has been Anne's good friend since their quarrel ended, and hopes for more than she has so far been willing to see.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: Anne's bosom friend from childhood, who has no wish for college and is quietly settling into the life Avonlea expects of her, with Fred Wright at her side. Comfortable and warm-hearted, she remains the person Anne writes to about everything, though the two lives are beginning to run on different lines.
characters.name: Diana Barry

characters.description: The mistress of Green Gables, growing older and no longer able for hard work, who runs the house with Mrs. Rachel Lynde and the twins about her. She parts with Anne for Redmond without a word of complaint and misses her more than she will say.
characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert

characters.description: Widowed and installed at Green Gables as housekeeper, she manages Marilla, the twins, and a good deal of Avonlea, and delivers her verdict on college for girls without waiting to be asked.
characters.name: Mrs. Rachel Lynde

characters.description: The orphan boy Marilla has brought up at Green Gables, now nine, still inquisitive and still in trouble, and the author of long, badly spelled letters that carry Avonlea news to Anne at college.
characters.name: Davy Keith

characters.description: A pretty, wealthy, and thoroughly frivolous freshman from Bolingbroke whom Anne meets in her first days at Redmond. She cannot decide anything, from a hat to a suitor, keeps a crowd of admirers she takes no more seriously than her hats, and is far cleverer than she pretends. She attaches herself to Anne at once.
characters.name: Philippa Gordon

characters.description: An Avonlea girl and Anne's friend from Queen's days, sensible and companionable, who goes to Redmond in the same year and shares Anne's lodgings and her explorations of Kingsport.
characters.name: Priscilla Grant

characters.description: A Redmond student from a Nova Scotia family, dark-eyed and dryly humorous, who joins Anne's circle and proposes the household arrangement that gives the girls a house of their own.
characters.name: Stella Maynard

characters.description: Stella's elderly aunt, a small, rosy, white-haired widow of a missionary who comes to keep house for the girls as their chaperone. Tolerant, shrewd, and untroubled by modern notions or by cats, she presides over the household with common sense and a warm hearth.
characters.name: Aunt Jamesina

characters.description: An Avonlea girl of Anne's own age, fair and pretty, absorbed since school days in her beaux and her good looks, and now teaching at a country school. Anne has always found her shallow company and is fond of her nonetheless.
characters.name: Ruby Gillis

characters.description: An Avonlea boy who has followed Anne to Redmond, solemn, self-satisfied, and afflicted with prominent eyes and the Sloane manner, entirely certain that his attentions must be welcome.
characters.name: Charlie Sloane

characters.description: A dark, handsome young man of a wealthy Kingsport family, who first speaks to Anne when he shelters her from a rainstorm. He is graceful, well read, and given to paying compliments in the language of poetry, and he answers almost exactly to the hero Anne has imagined since girlhood.
characters.name: Royal Gardner

characters.description: A striking Kingsport girl from a good family, an acquaintance of Gilbert's sister-in-law's people, who is often seen in Gilbert's company at Redmond social affairs.
characters.name: Christine Stuart

characters.description: A divinity student in charge of a small mission church near Kingsport, plain-faced, poor, and entirely without polish, but so good and so genuinely amusing that Philippa Gordon's crowd of handsome suitors cannot compete with him.
characters.name: Jonas Blake

characters.description: Anne's old pupil from Avonlea, now away at school in the United States with his father and stepmother, who writes to her and visits when he can, still full of the fancies that made him her favourite scholar.
characters.name: Paul Irving

recaps.ending: Anne takes her degree at Redmond, refuses Royal Gardner when he finally proposes because she discovers she has only been in love with an idea of him, and comes home to Avonlea for good. Philippa Gordon marries Jonas Blake and goes with him to his poor shore parish in a fishing village, entirely happy. Patty's Place is given up and Aunt Jamesina goes home. In Avonlea, Anne finds Gilbert changed and distant and hears that he is expected to marry Christine Stuart. Then Gilbert falls dangerously ill with typhoid fever, and during the night when the crisis is expected to kill him Anne understands that she has loved him all along and that her refusal of him was the great mistake of her life. He recovers, and when he is strong enough the two meet in the woods above Avonlea. Gilbert learns that Christine was never anything but a friend engaged to another man, and he asks Anne again. She accepts. They agree to wait three years while he completes his medical training, and Anne takes a teaching post to fill the time. Diana is married to Fred Wright, Green Gables is unchanged, and Anne ends the book engaged and at home.
recaps.in_short: Anne leaves Avonlea at eighteen for four years at Redmond College in Kingsport, where she makes friends with the frivolous, clever Philippa Gordon and eventually keeps house with her college friends at Patty's Place under the chaperonage of Aunt Jamesina. Childhood ends around her: Diana becomes engaged to Fred Wright, Anne refuses two absurd proposals and one serious one when Gilbert Blythe asks her to marry him, and her old schoolfellow Ruby Gillis dies of consumption. Estranged from Gilbert, Anne is courted by the handsome, poetic Royal Gardner and drifts into accepting his attentions, only to refuse him when he proposes, realizing that she wanted the romance rather than the man. She takes her degree, sees Philippa married to a poor divinity student, and returns to Avonlea. There Gilbert nearly dies of typhoid fever, and in the fear of losing him Anne discovers that she has loved him for years. He recovers, asks her again, and this time she accepts, on the understanding that they will wait three years for his medical course to end.

recaps.text: Previously: Anne Shirley came to Green Gables in Avonlea, on Prince Edward Island, as an eleven-year-old orphan sent by mistake to Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, who had asked for a boy. She stayed, grew up there, and made a bosom friend of Diana Barry and a long-running rival of the clever Gilbert Blythe. She won a place at Queen's Academy and a scholarship to Redmond College, but gave the scholarship up when Matthew died and Marilla's eyes began to fail, and taught the Avonlea school for two years instead, keeping house with Marilla. In that time Marilla took in the orphan twins Davy and Dora Keith, Anne helped an old quarrel between Miss Lavendar Lewis and Stephen Irving to a wedding, and her quarrel with Gilbert turned into friendship. When Mrs. Rachel Lynde was widowed she came to Green Gables to keep house, which set Anne free at last to take the college course she had put aside.

Anne is nearly nineteen, and change is coming to Avonlea. Diana becomes engaged to Fred Wright, which Anne struggles to reconcile with the romantic future she had imagined for her friend, and Anne herself prepares to leave for Redmond College in Kingsport, on the mainland. Marilla and Mrs. Lynde see her off; Gilbert Blythe, Charlie Sloane, and Priscilla Grant travel to Redmond too. Anne's first days at college are miserable with homesickness and the loneliness of being one unknown freshman among many. Her spirits recover when she is befriended by Philippa Gordon, a pretty, wealthy, and hopelessly indecisive girl from Bolingbroke who collects admirers as other people collect ribbons and who takes to Anne at once. Anne and Priscilla find rooms on St. John Street, explore the old graveyard and the park, and letters from home, chiefly Davy's, keep Avonlea close.

Anne finishes her freshman year and goes home to Avonlea for the summer, where Green Gables is unchanged and the twins are older but not much improved. She receives the first of a series of proposals: Jane Andrews's brother Billy sends Jane to ask on his behalf, and Anne refuses, astonished; Charlie Sloane, in due course, is refused as well. Back at Redmond the following autumn, Anne, Priscilla, Stella Maynard, and Philippa take a small house near the park called Patty's Place, complete with two china dogs on the mantel, rented from its elderly owners who are travelling abroad. Stella's aunt, a cheerful little widow known as Aunt Jamesina, comes to keep house for them, bringing her cats and her tolerant wisdom. The four girls settle into a household of their own, and their college years become a comfortable, busy round of study, visitors, and long evenings by the fire.

Anne, who has been writing stories, is persuaded to let Diana enter one of them in a competition; Diana submits it to a baking-powder company's contest without telling Anne how far she has altered it, and the story wins and is published with the product worked into the plot. Anne is mortified and gives up writing for a time. That summer at home brings a heavier grief. Ruby Gillis, Anne's old schoolfellow, is dying of consumption, though the village keeps up the pretence that she is merely delicate. Anne visits her and finds that Ruby, who has cared for nothing but parties and admirers, is terrified of dying and clings to the life she knows. In their last conversations Ruby speaks honestly for the first time in her life. She dies before the summer is out, and Anne, who has never been close to death since Matthew, returns to Redmond changed by it.

The friendship between Anne and Gilbert comes to a crisis. Gilbert tells Anne that he has loved her since their school days and asks her to marry him. Anne, who has always imagined that love would announce itself with a rush of feeling she has never had for Gilbert, refuses him, and the refusal wounds him deeply. Their easy companionship ends; Gilbert keeps away from her, and Anne is left unhappy without understanding why, since she is certain she was right. She goes home to Avonlea for the summer, where Green Gables, Marilla, the twins, and the old walks are a comfort, and where Paul Irving comes back on a visit. Philippa's letters keep her amused. Anne tells herself that she and Gilbert will be friends again in time, and the year turns without their being anything of the kind.

In Kingsport, Philippa astonishes everyone, herself included, by falling in love with Jonas Blake, a poor, plain divinity student in charge of a mission church, and losing interest in her wealthy suitors. Anne, sheltering from a rainstorm, meets Royal Gardner, a dark, handsome young man of a rich Kingsport family who talks like the hero of her girlhood dreams. He courts her steadily, and Anne, flattered and half persuaded, lets the courtship run on while telling herself that this must be what she has waited for. At Redmond she sees Gilbert frequently in the company of Christine Stuart and concludes that he has transferred his affections; the old ease between them does not come back. In Avonlea, Diana marries Fred Wright with Anne as bridesmaid, and Anne watches her friend settle into a plain, contented happiness quite unlike anything in her own imaginings.

Anne spends a summer boarding at Valley Road while teaching there, and takes a hand in the affairs of her landlady, who has been courted for twenty years by a man too much under his mother's thumb to speak; when he finally does, Anne has had something to do with it. Back at Redmond for her final year, she is treated by everyone, including herself, as good as engaged to Royal Gardner, and his formidable mother and sisters call on her and inspect her thoroughly. Philippa is settled in her own mind about Jonas, whatever her family may say. The household at Patty's Place goes on through its last winter, with Aunt Jamesina presiding and the cats before the fire, and Anne is aware that a whole way of life is ending. She has still not admitted to herself what she felt when she refused Gilbert Blythe.

Roy Gardner makes his proposal in the setting he has carefully chosen, and Anne hears herself refuse him and knows at once that she is right: she has been in love with a picture of a lover, not with the man. Roy is bitterly offended, and Anne is left feeling foolish. She and Gilbert both take their degrees; Patty's Place is given back to its owners, Aunt Jamesina goes home, and Philippa marries Jonas Blake and goes off entirely happy to his poor shore parish. Anne returns to Avonlea for good, hearing on all sides that Gilbert Blythe is expected to marry Christine Stuart. Then Gilbert falls ill with typhoid fever, and the village waits through a night in which the doctors expect him to die. Sitting alone, Anne understands that she has loved him for years and that her refusal was the great mistake of her life. Word comes in the morning that the crisis has passed. When he is well enough to walk out, the two meet in the woods above Avonlea; Gilbert explains that Christine was never more than a friend, engaged all along to another man, and asks Anne again. She accepts, and they agree to wait three years while he finishes his medical course.

characters.description: Newly graduated from Redmond and engaged to Gilbert Blythe, she has come to the harbour town of Summerside as principal of the high school for the three years he will spend at medical school. She boards at Windy Poplars, an old house in Spook's Lane, and writes Gilbert long letters that carry most of the story. Warm, curious, and incurably interested in other people's affairs, she makes friends easily everywhere except in the one quarter where it matters most.
characters.name: Anne Shirley

characters.description: Anne's fiance, away at medical school on the mainland for the three years of her Summerside appointment. He appears almost entirely as the recipient of her letters, and the engagement is a private happiness she keeps largely to herself.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: The general help at Windy Poplars, a short, stout woman of decided views who considers herself the real head of the household while insisting she is only the servant. She conducts loud arguments with the cat, guards the widows' comfort fiercely, and takes Anne into her confidence within a week.
characters.name: Rebecca Dew

characters.description: One of the two elderly widows who keep Windy Poplars, the elder and the sterner, sensible and reserved, who does not care for cats and takes a while to unbend to a young lodger.
characters.name: Aunt Kate

characters.description: The younger of the two widows at Windy Poplars, softer than her sister and easily hurt, given to weeping over slights and to small conspiracies with Anne behind Aunt Kate's back.
characters.name: Aunt Chatty

characters.description: A solemn, fair-haired little girl of about eight who lives in the great house next door with her grandmother and an unsmiling housekeeper, and who is allowed almost nothing. She gets her milk from Windy Poplars and befriends Anne over the garden gate. She has invented a place called Tomorrow, in which everything she wants will happen, including the arrival of the father she has never known, and she gives herself a different name for every mood.
characters.name: Little Elizabeth Grayson

characters.description: Elizabeth's grandmother, a rigid, formal old woman who took the child in after her mother's death, keeps her strictly, and permits no friendships or indulgences in the house she rules.
characters.name: Mrs. Campbell

characters.description: The vice-principal of Summerside High School, a dark, angular young woman with a harsh voice and no friends, who had expected the principalship herself and makes no attempt to hide her resentment. She rejects every civility Anne offers and is disliked throughout the town.
characters.name: Katherine Brooke

characters.description: A clever, pretty, insolent pupil in Anne's school and a member of the town's dominant family, who leads the classroom campaign against the new principal on the clan's behalf.
characters.name: Jen Pringle

characters.description: Two elderly sisters who are the acknowledged heads of the Pringle clan, which is related to half of Summerside. Courteous in manner and implacable in fact, they have decided that Anne shall not keep her post, and the whole connection follows their lead.
characters.name: Miss Sarah and Miss Ellen Pringle

characters.description: A middle-aged Summerside woman kept in near-servitude by a demanding invalid mother, who has not been allowed an afternoon to herself in years and would like to attend an old friend's silver wedding.
characters.name: Pauline Gibson

characters.description: A pretty, pliable Summerside girl engaged to Jarvis Morrow, whose father forbids the match for reasons nobody can discover, and who has not the resolution to settle the matter either way.
characters.name: Dovie Westcott

characters.description: A Summerside youth working his way through school by selling photographs and doing odd jobs, cheerful about his poverty, who becomes Anne's companion on country rambles.
characters.name: Lewis Allen

characters.description: One of the Nelson sisters, dark and proud and no longer young, who has quarrelled with the man she loves and would rather be thought indifferent than admit she is unhappy.
characters.name: Nora Nelson

characters.description: The last of a once-great Summerside family, living alone in the large, gloomy Tomgallon house, who takes a sombre pride in the many tragedies of her relations and recites them to guests over dinner.
characters.name: Miss Minerva Tomgallon

recaps.ending: Anne finishes her third year as principal of Summerside High School and resigns to be married. The Pringle clan, long since won over, is sorry to lose her. Katherine Brooke, whose bitterness Anne dissolved by taking her home to Green Gables for Christmas, has left teaching for work she actually wants and has become a real friend. Little Elizabeth's future is settled: Anne brings her father, Pierce Grayson, to see her, the misunderstanding that kept them apart is cleared up, and Elizabeth goes to live with him, so that the Tomorrow she has been waiting for arrives at last. Anne makes her farewells at Windy Poplars, where Rebecca Dew and the two widows part from her with real grief, and she leaves Spook's Lane for the last time. Miss Minerva Tomgallon's house, the Summerside gossip, the school, and the three years of letters are behind her; ahead is her wedding to Gilbert Blythe, who has finished his medical course, and the house by the sea they will begin their marriage in. The book closes with Anne's Summerside chapter shut and her married life about to begin.
recaps.in_short: Engaged to Gilbert Blythe and waiting out his medical course, Anne Shirley spends three years as principal of Summerside High School, boarding at an old house called Windy Poplars with two elderly widows and their outspoken help, Rebecca Dew. The story is told largely through her letters to Gilbert. Her first year is a quiet war with the Pringles, the clan that dominates the town and resents her appointment, until an old family diary comes into her hands and the opposition collapses. She wears down the hostility of the embittered vice-principal Katherine Brooke by taking her home to Green Gables for Christmas, and befriends a lonely, strictly reared child next door, little Elizabeth Grayson, who is waiting for a father she has never met. Between these threads Anne meddles benevolently in Summerside's romances, feuds, and family histories. At the end of the three years she reunites Elizabeth with her father, resigns her post, and leaves Summerside to be married.

recaps.text: Previously: Anne Shirley grew up at Green Gables in Avonlea, on Prince Edward Island, after being sent there as an orphan child by mistake to Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert. She taught the village school for two years, then took her degree at Redmond College in Kingsport, where she refused Gilbert Blythe's first proposal, was courted for a while by the handsome Royal Gardner, and lost her old schoolfellow Ruby Gillis to consumption. When Gilbert nearly died of typhoid fever she understood that she had loved him all along, and on his recovery they became engaged, agreeing to wait three years while he finished his medical training. Her closest friend Diana is married to Fred Wright and living near Avonlea; Marilla keeps Green Gables with Mrs. Rachel Lynde and the twins, Davy and Dora. This book covers those three waiting years, which Anne spends away from home.

Anne arrives in Summerside as principal of the high school and takes a room at Windy Poplars, an old house in Spook's Lane kept by two elderly widows, Aunt Kate and Aunt Chatty, with their formidable help Rebecca Dew and a much-disputed cat. She is comfortable there at once. The school is another matter. The Pringles, a clan connected to half the town, had wanted the principalship for one of their own and set themselves to drive Anne out: her pupils are politely unteachable, Jen Pringle is quietly insolent, and invitations dry up. The vice-principal, Katherine Brooke, who wanted the post herself, refuses every friendly approach and is openly hostile. Anne also meets little Elizabeth Grayson from the great house next door, a lonely, closely guarded child who comes for the milk, calls herself by a different name each day, and lives for a time she calls Tomorrow, when her absent father will come for her.

The Pringle campaign continues through the autumn, and Anne, who has never failed to make friends anywhere, finds the situation wearing. Calling on an elderly woman on an errand of neighbourly kindness, she is given an old handwritten diary kept by a seafaring member of the family, and reading it discovers a discreditable truth about the ancestor the Pringles revere above all others. Anne has no intention of using it, but once the two elderly sisters who head the clan learn that she has read it, the resistance ends overnight. Invitations arrive, Jen Pringle becomes an ordinary pupil, and the school settles down. Anne fills the rest of her first year with the affairs of Summerside: neighbours' feuds, courtships, old family grievances, and the friendship of little Elizabeth, whose grandmother allows the child almost nothing and whom Anne takes on rare and treasured walks.

In her second year Anne is established in Summerside and busy in other people's lives. She helps a young couple whose engagement has been forbidden by an unreasonable father, contriving matters so that the pair settle the question themselves; she gives a woman kept in service to a tyrannical invalid mother a single afternoon of freedom at a friend's silver wedding; she takes country walks with Lewis Allen, a poor student working his way through school, and blunders cheerfully into more than one household's private history. The important change of the year is Katherine Brooke. Anne persuades her to spend Christmas at Green Gables, and away from Summerside the vice-principal's hardness gives way; she tells Anne about a childhood of poverty and charity and dependence, and gradually becomes a friend. Katherine afterwards leaves teaching, which she has always hated, for work she has chosen for herself.

Anne's third and last year in Summerside brings more of the town's tangled affairs. She dines at the gloomy Tomgallon house with its last surviving daughter, who recounts the disasters of her family with mournful relish; she has a hand in reconciling a proud woman with the man she quarrelled with years ago; and she watches over little Elizabeth, whose grandmother's rule grows no gentler. The child's situation troubles Anne more and more, and she resolves to do something about the father who has left her there.

Anne discovers what has kept Elizabeth's father away: he blamed the child for her mother's death and has been discouraged from claiming her. Anne writes to him, and when Pierce Grayson comes to Summerside she brings father and daughter together. The misunderstanding is cleared away, Mrs. Campbell's hold on the child is broken, and Elizabeth is to live with her father, so the Tomorrow she has been waiting for finally arrives. Anne's third year at the school ends. She resigns her post to be married, and the Pringles, who once tried to drive her out, are among those sorriest to see her go. Katherine Brooke is settled and happy in a new life. The parting at Windy Poplars is hard on everyone, Rebecca Dew and the two widows most of all, and Anne leaves Spook's Lane for the last time. Gilbert has finished his medical course; the three years of waiting are over, and Anne goes home to be married.

characters.description: Twenty-five, and about to be married at Green Gables after three years of waiting. She leaves Avonlea for Four Winds Harbour, where Gilbert has taken over a country practice, and sets up house in a small white cottage on the shore that she names her house of dreams. Still the girl who renames the places she loves, she is now a young wife making friends in a community of fishermen, farmers, and sailors, and she has never yet had to bear a real sorrow of her own.
characters.name: Anne Blythe

characters.description: Newly qualified as a doctor and about to marry Anne, he takes over an established country practice at Four Winds and Glen St. Mary. Steady, hard-working, and conscientious to the point of stubbornness where his profession is concerned, he holds that a doctor's duty is to cure whoever can be cured.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: The keeper of the Four Winds light, an old sailor with a weather-beaten face and remarkably young blue eyes, who has spent a lifetime at sea and can tell the story of every wreck on the coast. He keeps a lighthouse, a cat called the First Mate, and a store of tales he has never written down, and he takes to Anne and Gilbert from their first evening at the point.
characters.name: Captain Jim Boyd

characters.description: A capable, plain-spoken spinster of the harbour who calls on Anne early and stays to give her the history of everyone in it. She keeps up a lifelong quarrel with men and Methodists, does more practical good than anyone else in the community, and will sew for a neighbour's baby while explaining exactly what is wrong with its father.
characters.name: Miss Cornelia Bryant

characters.description: A strikingly beautiful young woman who lives in the grey house up the harbour and drives her geese along the shore road. She is about Anne's age, proud and cold to strangers, and refuses friendliness so firmly that Anne almost gives her up. Something in her life has shut her away from her neighbours, and the harbour speaks of her with pity.
characters.name: Leslie Moore

characters.description: Leslie's husband, a big, bearded man who went to sea years ago and was brought home from Cuba after a fever and a head injury with his memory and his wits gone. He is docile, childish, and entirely dependent, and Leslie has cared for him ever since.
characters.name: Dick Moore
