characters.description: A tall, bearded man of the harbour, prosperous and well liked, who swore years ago that he would neither shave nor cut his hair until his political party won an election, and has kept the vow long past the point where anyone remembers him otherwise.
characters.name: Marshall Elliott

characters.description: A journalist and writer from Toronto who comes to Four Winds for the summer and boards with the Moores. His grandparents were the schoolmaster and his bride for whom Anne's little house was built, so the place has a hold on him. Easy company, observant, and looking for a book he can write.
characters.name: Owen Ford

characters.description: A middle-aged Glen St. Mary woman engaged to help in the Blythe household, devoted, thoroughly competent, and possessed of firm opinions on cooking, children, and her neighbours' failings. She attaches herself to the family at once and regards its concerns as her own.
characters.name: Susan Baker

characters.description: The mistress of Green Gables, old now and quiet, who gives Anne away from the house she came to as a child and afterwards keeps the farm with Mrs. Lynde and the twins.
characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert

characters.description: Housekeeper at Green Gables and Avonlea's chief authority on everything, who superintends the wedding preparations and is not shy of saying what she thinks of the arrangements.
characters.name: Mrs. Rachel Lynde

characters.description: Anne's oldest friend, now Mrs. Fred Wright, settled near Avonlea with a young family and as fond of Anne as ever, though the two see each other only when Anne comes home.
characters.name: Diana Wright

characters.description: The elderly doctor at Glen St. Mary whose practice Gilbert is taking over, and his wife, long fixtures of the district, who welcome the young couple to Four Winds and hand on a lifetime of local knowledge.
characters.name: Doctor Dave

characters.description: A son born to Anne and Gilbert at the little house, named for two men they loved, a healthy, vigorous baby who fills the house of dreams and is adored by the whole household.
characters.name: James Matthew Blythe

recaps.ending: The truth about Leslie Moore's husband frees her: the man she nursed for years was Dick Moore's cousin George, and the real Dick died abroad long ago, so her marriage never existed. Owen Ford returns to Four Winds and the two become engaged. Anne and Gilbert's son, James Matthew, is born safely and thrives, with Susan Baker installed to help in the house. Captain Jim's life-book, written up by Owen from the old man's stories, is published; Captain Jim reads his copy through on a quiet evening at the light and is found dead in his chair, having gone out as easily as a ship crossing the bar, with the First Mate beside him. Miss Cornelia Bryant, after a lifetime of denouncing men, marries Marshall Elliott, who shaves at last. Leslie and Owen marry and take the little house on the shore as their own summer home, so it stays in loving hands. Gilbert's practice has grown too large for the cottage, and he and Anne move up to a big house at Glen St. Mary called Ingleside, taking Susan and the baby with them. Anne leaves her house of dreams with real grief and with the certainty that the happiness it held goes with her.
recaps.in_short: Anne Shirley marries Gilbert Blythe at Green Gables and goes to keep house in a small cottage on Four Winds Harbour, where Gilbert has taken over a country practice. Her neighbours are the old lighthouse keeper Captain Jim, the outspoken Miss Cornelia Bryant, and Leslie Moore, a beautiful young woman married at sixteen to a man who came home from sea with his wits gone and who has nursed him ever since. Anne wins Leslie's friendship slowly, and their first real closeness comes after Anne's baby daughter is born and dies within a day. A writer named Owen Ford comes to board with the Moores, takes down Captain Jim's life story for a book, and falls in love with Leslie, which seems hopeless. Gilbert then argues that Leslie's husband might be cured by surgery. The operation reveals that the man is not Dick Moore at all but his cousin; the real Dick died years before, and Leslie is free. Leslie and Owen marry, Anne's son Jem is born, Captain Jim dies the night he reads his finished book, and the Blythes move to a larger house at Glen St. Mary.

recaps.text: Previously: Anne Shirley was sent as an orphan child to Green Gables in Avonlea, on Prince Edward Island, and grew up there with Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert. She taught the village school, took her degree at Redmond College, and after refusing Gilbert Blythe once became engaged to him when he nearly died of typhoid fever. She then spent three years as principal of Summerside High School while Gilbert studied medicine, boarding at Windy Poplars and gradually winning over a hostile town. Her old friend Diana is married to Fred Wright; Marilla keeps Green Gables with Mrs. Rachel Lynde and the twins Davy and Dora. Gilbert has now qualified as a doctor. This book opens with their wedding, and moves the story away from Avonlea to Four Winds Harbour, where the young couple begin married life.

Anne is married to Gilbert Blythe in the orchard at Green Gables, the first bride the old house has sent out, with Diana, Marilla, Mrs. Lynde, and the twins about her and a household of old friends looking on. The couple travel to Four Winds Harbour, sixty miles away, where Gilbert is taking over the country practice of the elderly Doctor Dave. Their home is a small white house on the shore below the Glen, sheltered by poplars, with a brook and a garden planted by a bride of long ago. Anne learns its history: it was built by a young schoolmaster for the girl he brought home from Scotland, and it has held a series of happy marriages ever since. She calls it her house of dreams, arranges her own things in it, and looks out at the harbour, the sand bar, and the lighthouse on the point with the feeling that her real life has just begun.

Anne and Gilbert make the acquaintance of their neighbours. Captain Jim, the keeper of the Four Winds light, is an old sailor with a lifetime of stories and no words to write them down; he adopts the young couple, and his lighthouse becomes their favourite evening walk. Miss Cornelia Bryant calls and stays to explain the harbour, its history, its Methodists, and the general uselessness of men, while sewing for somebody else's baby. Anne is haunted by the beautiful young woman she has glimpsed driving geese along the shore, Leslie Moore of the grey house up the harbour, who rebuffs every friendly approach. Miss Cornelia tells her the story: Leslie's brother was killed as a child, her father took his own life, and at sixteen she married a man she disliked to save her mother's home. He went to sea, and was brought back from Cuba after a fever and a blow to the head with his mind gone. She has nursed him ever since.

Leslie comes down to the little house at last, and the friendship Anne wanted begins, though it is uneven; Leslie is warm one week and shut away the next, and Anne does not always understand why. A first winter at Four Winds passes with storms, firelight, Christmas at the Glen, and New Year's Eve at the lighthouse, where Captain Jim tells his stories and Miss Cornelia gives her opinions. Anne hears more of the harbour's people and their histories, including a suggestion that Captain Jim once loved a girl who was lost at sea. Spring comes to the shore, and Anne is quietly happy, with the garden coming out and the harbour blue again. She is expecting her first child, and the little house is made ready for it.

Anne's baby, a daughter they name Joyce, is born and lives only a day. Anne's grief is the first real sorrow of her life, and it changes the house of dreams for her. It is Leslie Moore who comes to her, and out of that shared trouble the last barrier between the two women goes down; from then on they are close friends without reserve. Anne slowly recovers, and Captain Jim, who has known his own losses, tells her the story of the girl he waited for who never came back from the sea. That summer a visitor arrives at Four Winds: Owen Ford, a Toronto journalist, who turns out to be the grandson of the schoolmaster and the bride for whom Anne's little house was built. He boards with the Moores. Hearing Captain Jim's stories, Anne sees that they are a book waiting to be written, and Owen agrees to write it from the old man's own life-book of notes.

Owen Ford works on Captain Jim's life-book through the summer, and the harbour, the lighthouse, and the little house are full of company and talk. Owen and Leslie fall in love. Owen tells Anne of it before he goes away, and Leslie, who cannot be free while her husband lives, is left wretched, having found and lost the one chance of happiness she thought she had given up. Gilbert then raises a possibility that Anne would rather not hear: he believes that the injury to Dick Moore's head might be relieved by surgery, and that a specialist could restore him. Anne argues fiercely against telling Leslie, since a cured husband would only fasten the marriage on her more surely; Gilbert answers that a doctor cannot suppress a chance of cure to suit anybody's happiness. Leslie is told and, after a struggle, decides to go through with it. The operation reveals that the man is not Dick Moore at all, but his cousin George, who resembled him. The real Dick died of fever in Cuba years ago, and Leslie has never been a wife at all.

George Moore, restored to himself and with no memory of the lost years, is sent back to his own people. Leslie is free at last, but she believes Owen Ford gone for good and will not write to him, and the autumn is a wretched one for her. Owen returns to Four Winds of his own accord, learns the truth, and he and Leslie become engaged. Anne's second child, a son, is born safely at the little house and named James Matthew for Captain Jim and for Matthew Cuthbert; Susan Baker comes from the Glen to help with the house and takes charge of the family's affairs as though she had been born to them. Captain Jim, who has waited to see the boy, is content. The life-book of his stories, written up by Owen, is going through the press, and the old man speaks of it as the one thing he still wants to see finished.

The life-book is published under Owen's name with Captain Jim's stories at its heart, and the old man is deeply happy with it. He reads his copy through on a quiet evening at the lighthouse and is found next morning dead in his chair, with his hand on the book and the First Mate beside him; the harbour buries him as a man everyone loved. Miss Cornelia Bryant then astonishes the district by announcing that she is to marry Marshall Elliott, who cuts his hair and shaves off the beard he grew for a political vow, and the wedding duly takes place. Leslie Moore and Owen Ford are married and take the little house on the shore for their own, which spares Anne the pain of leaving it to strangers. Gilbert's practice at Glen St. Mary has outgrown the cottage, and he has bought a big old house up at the Glen called Ingleside. Anne says goodbye to her house of dreams, grieving for it and for Captain Jim, and moves up to the Glen with Gilbert, little Jem, and Susan Baker.

characters.description: A young Black jazz drummer in New York whose talent and charm have not protected him from poverty, racism, or a deepening personal crisis. Estranged from friends and haunted by the collapse of his relationship with Leona, he moves through the city in a state of exhaustion and despair.
characters.name: Rufus Scott

characters.description: Rufus's closest white friend, an aspiring novelist from Brooklyn. He is affectionate and loyal but often fails to grasp the racial pressures shaping Rufus's life. His earnestness, sexual uncertainty, and wish to see himself as open-minded are repeatedly tested by the people closest to him.
characters.name: Vivaldo Moore

characters.description: A white woman from the American South who came to New York after leaving a troubled marriage. Her intense relationship with Rufus crosses racial boundaries but is damaged by his jealousy, violence, and the hostility directed at them as a couple.
characters.name: Leona

characters.description: A successful novelist and Vivaldo's older friend. Married to Cass and raising two sons, he has begun to enjoy the public rewards of his career, while his confidence and absorption in work leave strains in his household that he does not fully recognize.
characters.name: Richard Silenski

characters.description: Richard's intelligent, perceptive wife and the mother of their children. She has supported his writing for years, but his recent success sharpens her sense that domestic life has narrowed her own possibilities.
characters.name: Cass Silenski

characters.description: Rufus's younger sister, a singer who meets his friends while grieving his death. Proud, wary, and sharply conscious of racial condescension, she is drawn to Vivaldo while questioning whether he can understand either her anger or her vulnerability.
characters.name: Ida Scott

characters.description: An American actor returning to New York after years in France. He once moved in the same circle as Rufus, Vivaldo, Richard, and Cass. More at ease with his attraction to men than he was in youth, he comes home while waiting for his younger lover, Yves, to join him.
characters.name: Eric Jones

characters.description: Eric's young French lover, first known through Eric's memories and their life together in the south of France. He plans to follow Eric to New York, making their separation a test of whether the security they found together can survive a new setting.
characters.name: Yves

characters.description: A successful, older television producer who takes an interest in Ida and can help her singing career. His access to money and influence places her ambitions within a relationship marked by unequal power.
characters.name: Ellis

characters.description: The young son of Richard and Cass, growing up amid tensions his parents try to keep outside the household.
characters.name: Paul Silenski

recaps.ending: Ida finally tells Vivaldo about her affair with Ellis and about the compromises, anger, and humiliation bound up with it. Her confession forces both of them to face how often their relationship has depended on partial truths and on Vivaldo's confidence that love alone can erase racial difference. Cass admits her relationship with Eric to Richard, leaving their marriage badly shaken but no longer protected by silence. Eric, having offered intimacy to both Cass and Vivaldo during his return, goes to meet Yves when the young man arrives from France. Their reunion closes the novel on a fragile possibility of tenderness rather than a settled resolution. Rufus remains the absent center of the group: his death cannot be repaired, and the surviving characters carry forward the conflicts over race, desire, guilt, and honesty that he exposed.
recaps.in_short: In New York, Black jazz drummer Rufus Scott falls into poverty and despair after his destructive interracial relationship with Leona ends, and he dies by suicide. His death binds together and unsettles those around him: his white friend Vivaldo begins a difficult relationship with Rufus's sister Ida; married Cass Silenski confronts the emptiness beneath her husband Richard's literary success; and actor Eric Jones returns from France while awaiting his lover Yves. As the characters seek intimacy across divisions of race, sex, and social power, they repeatedly conceal what they most need to say. Cass and Eric become lovers, Eric also shares a charged encounter with Vivaldo, and Ida becomes involved with the influential television producer Ellis while trying to advance as a singer. Ida eventually confesses the affair to Vivaldo, and Cass tells Richard the truth. Their relationships remain uncertain. Eric meets Yves on his arrival in New York, ending the novel with reunion and hope shadowed by the damage the group has done and endured.

recaps.text: Rufus Scott, a Black jazz drummer, wanders New York broke, hungry, and increasingly isolated. His memories return to Leona, a white Southern woman with whom he began an intense affair. Racist hostility from strangers and Rufus's own fear and rage poisoned the relationship; he became violent, and Leona suffered a breakdown before being taken away. Vivaldo Moore, Rufus's white friend and an aspiring writer, tries to help when they meet again, but Rufus cannot accept sustained care or imagine a way back into ordinary life. The city that once promised music and freedom has become a landscape of rejection, and his private despair is inseparable from the racial humiliations he has absorbed.

Rufus dies by jumping from the George Washington Bridge. Vivaldo and the Silenskis are left to examine their memories of him and the limits of the help they offered. At the funeral, Vivaldo meets Rufus's younger sister Ida. Grief brings them together, but Rufus's fate also stands between them: Ida knows how easily white friends can claim innocence about suffering they did not understand. Vivaldo is attracted to her and wants closeness, while she remains alert to his assumptions. Richard's growing success as a novelist, meanwhile, has not given Cass a comparable sense of purpose; the marriage appears secure from outside but is becoming emotionally unequal.

The focus widens after Rufus's death. Vivaldo and Ida begin a love affair, moving between genuine tenderness and arguments about race, jealousy, and the meanings each assigns to Rufus. Eric Jones, an actor who knew the group years earlier, returns from France for work. Abroad he has built a life with Yves, a younger Frenchman who is expected to follow him to New York. Eric's return reconnects him with Cass and Richard and revives old emotional possibilities. Cass feels increasingly unseen within Richard's success and recognizes in Eric someone willing to listen without reducing her to a wife and mother.

Ida pursues a singing career and attracts the attention of Ellis, an older television producer whose professional influence gives him power over her prospects. Vivaldo senses that she is withholding something, and their quarrels expose both his jealousy and his incomplete understanding of the pressures she faces as a Black woman. Cass and Eric grow closer and begin an affair. For Cass, the relationship is tied to a hunger for a self beyond Richard's household; for Eric, it complicates the commitment he has made to Yves. Richard remains largely unaware of how far his marriage has drifted from the story he tells himself about it.

The group's hidden lives begin to collide. Cass cannot indefinitely separate her affair with Eric from her marriage. Eric, whose sexuality once frightened him, is more candid than the others about desire but is still capable of causing pain while waiting for Yves. He and Vivaldo share an intimate encounter that unsettles Vivaldo's fixed ideas about himself. Ida's involvement with Ellis deepens the mistrust between her and Vivaldo. What began as several attempts to escape loneliness now requires each person to choose between further concealment and disclosures that may end the relationships they hoped to save.

Ida tells Vivaldo that she has been involved with Ellis, describing the mixture of ambition, coercive inequality, anger, and self-betrayal surrounding the affair. The confession does not settle whether she and Vivaldo can remain together, but it removes the illusion that he can understand their love without confronting race and power. Cass tells Richard about Eric, forcing the crisis in their marriage into the open. Eric prepares to receive Yves, aware that his encounters in New York have tested the life they planned. He meets Yves when he arrives, and their reunion offers the novel's clearest surviving possibility of trust. Rufus's death remains unresolved for everyone: the others move forward, but none can separate their new honesty from the loss that first drew them together.

characters.description: The younger daughter of Oedipus, slight, intense, and unwilling to accept King Creon's order that her brother Polynices remain unburied. She is engaged to Creon's son Haemon but places an absolute duty to the dead above safety and ordinary happiness.
characters.name: Antigone

characters.description: Antigone's older sister, beautiful, sociable, and more cautious. She understands why Antigone wants to honor Polynices but fears the death penalty and initially urges her sister to obey Creon's decree.
characters.name: Ismene

characters.description: The king of Thebes, Antigone's uncle, and Haemon's father. A practical ruler burdened by the work of restoring order after civil war, he has forbidden burial of Polynices as a public warning against rebellion.
characters.name: Creon

characters.description: Creon's son and Antigone's fiancé. Gentle and devoted to Antigone, he chose her unexpectedly over Ismene and imagines a future with her that her act of defiance places in danger.
characters.name: Haemon

characters.description: The elderly servant who raised Antigone and Ismene. Maternal, anxious, and concerned with everyday needs, she mistakes Antigone's secret early-morning excursion for a romantic meeting.
characters.name: Nurse

characters.description: A theatrical commentator who introduces the cast, explains the fatal pattern already enclosing them, and periodically interprets the action for the audience. The Chorus presents tragedy as an unavoidable mechanism once it has begun.
characters.name: Chorus

characters.description: One of the ordinary soldiers assigned to watch Polynices' body. More worried about punishment, promotion, and routine comforts than questions of justice, he reports the attempted burial to Creon and later helps arrest Antigone.
characters.name: First Guard

characters.description: Creon's wife and Haemon's mother. She spends much of the action quietly knitting, an image of contained domestic life set against the public conflict consuming her family.
characters.name: Eurydice

characters.description: The young attendant who accompanies Creon and observes the king's exhausting official duties. His presence emphasizes the ordinary life and future that continue beyond the tragedy.
characters.name: Page

recaps.ending: Creon orders Antigone sealed in a cave, then belatedly goes to release her after the Chorus warns that he has pushed the punishment too far. He arrives after Antigone has hanged herself. Haemon, found holding her body, rejects his father and kills himself. A messenger brings the news to Eurydice, who quietly withdraws and cuts her throat. Creon is left alive after losing his wife, his son, and his niece. He returns to the administrative work of the state because, unlike Antigone, he has accepted the duty of continuing. The guards resume their card game, untouched by the royal family's destruction, and the Chorus closes the play on the silence that follows tragedy.
recaps.in_short: After the sons of Oedipus kill each other in a civil war, Creon honors Eteocles and forbids burial of Polynices. Their sister Antigone secretly covers Polynices' body with earth and is arrested when she returns to perform the rite again. Creon tries privately to save his niece, arguing that rule is practical work and revealing that neither brother deserves her idealized loyalty. Antigone nearly accepts life but rejects the compromised happiness he offers and insists on owning her act. Creon condemns her to be sealed in a cave. She hangs herself before he can reverse course; her fiancé Haemon, Creon's son, kills himself beside her, and Creon's wife Eurydice takes her own life after hearing the news. Creon survives and returns alone to governing while the indifferent guards carry on with their routine.

recaps.text: After civil war in Thebes, the brothers Eteocles and Polynices have killed each other. Their uncle Creon becomes king, gives Eteocles an honored funeral, and orders that the supposed traitor Polynices be left exposed on pain of death. Antigone has already scattered earth over Polynices and returns to complete the burial despite her sister Ismene's refusal to help. Guards catch her and bring her to Creon. Hoping to avoid a scandal and save his son's fiancée, Creon questions her privately and offers to conceal the crime. He argues that governing requires imperfect choices and tells her the brothers were both corrupt, their ruined bodies so alike that the official distinction between hero and traitor was arbitrary. Antigone briefly wavers but refuses the modest, compromised happiness Creon describes. She insists on accepting the consequence of her deliberate act. Ismene then asks to share her fate, but Antigone refuses her late claim. Creon has Antigone sealed in a cave. She dictates a last message to Haemon and then removes the words that express doubt. The Chorus persuades Creon to free her, but he is too late: Antigone has hanged herself. Haemon kills himself beside her, and Eurydice takes her own life after learning their fate. Creon, stripped of his family, resumes the work of ruling, while the guards return to their cards.

characters.description: A daughter of Oedipus and sister of the two princes who have killed each other in the struggle for Thebes. She is determined to give Polynices the burial rites that Creon has forbidden, placing divine obligation and family loyalty above obedience to the new king.
characters.name: Antigone

characters.description: Antigone's sister and the other surviving daughter of Oedipus. She fears the power of the state and initially refuses to help bury Polynices, although her caution comes from concern for Antigone as well as concern for herself.
characters.name: Ismene

characters.description: The new king of Thebes and uncle of Antigone, Ismene, Polynices, and Eteocles. Intent on restoring civic order after civil war, he honors Eteocles as a defender and prohibits burial of Polynices as a traitor. He treats resistance to the decree as a challenge to royal authority.
characters.name: Creon

characters.description: Creon's son and Antigone's intended husband. He approaches his father respectfully, then argues that Theban opinion favors Antigone and that a ruler should be willing to listen and change course.
characters.name: Haemon

characters.description: An elderly blind prophet whose guidance Creon has trusted before. Led by a young attendant, he reports ominous failures in sacrifice and warns that the gods reject Thebes' treatment of Polynices and Antigone.
characters.name: Tiresias

characters.description: A nervous sentry assigned to watch the unburied body of Polynices. He brings Creon unwelcome news that someone has performed burial rites, then returns after the guards catch Antigone repeating the act.
characters.name: The Guard

characters.description: Creon's wife and Haemon's mother. She appears late, hears the messenger's account of the disaster involving her son, and withdraws into the palace without public display.
characters.name: Eurydice

characters.description: The representative voice of the group of Theban elders who observe the conflict. He receives reports, questions the principals, and eventually urges Creon to follow Tiresias's warning without delay.
characters.name: Chorus Leader

characters.description: A palace messenger who reports the consequences of Creon's delayed reversal, describing what happened at Polynices' body and at Antigone's sealed tomb.
characters.name: Messenger

recaps.ending: Tiresias warns that the gods hold Creon responsible for leaving Polynices unburied and confining Antigone alive. Shaken at last, Creon arranges the burial and goes to release Antigone, but his reversal comes too late. Antigone has hanged herself in the tomb. Haemon, grieving beside her, attacks his father and then kills himself. When Eurydice hears that her son is dead, she also takes her own life, cursing Creon as responsible. Creon returns carrying Haemon's body and learns of his wife's death. His decree has not secured his family or the city; it has left him alive, stripped of wife and son, and conscious that his own obstinacy caused the ruin. The elders close on the lesson that proud judgment without reverence brings punishment and that wisdom is learned through suffering.
recaps.in_short: After civil war in Thebes, the new king, Creon, orders that Eteocles be honored but that his brother Polynices be left unburied as a traitor. Their sister Antigone obeys religious and family duty instead, performs burial rites, and openly accepts responsibility when caught. Creon rejects the pleas of Ismene, his son Haemon, and the Theban elders, sentencing Antigone to be sealed alive in a rocky tomb. The prophet Tiresias warns that the gods reject Creon's treatment of the dead and that his own household will pay for it. Creon finally yields, buries Polynices, and goes to free Antigone, but she has already hanged herself. Haemon dies by suicide beside her, and his mother Eurydice kills herself after hearing the news. Creon survives to recognize that his inflexible assertion of authority has destroyed his family.

recaps.text: The brothers Eteocles and Polynices have killed one another while fighting over Thebes. Creon, the new king, grants Eteocles an honorable burial but decrees that Polynices must remain exposed as an enemy of the city. Antigone tells Ismene that she will defy the order and give their brother the rites owed to the dead. A guard later reports that someone has covered the body, and Antigone is caught when she returns. She admits what she did and argues that Creon's command cannot overrule divine law. Ismene offers to share her fate, but Antigone refuses to let her claim a deed she would not join. Creon condemns Antigone despite her engagement to his son. Haemon warns his father that Thebes sympathizes with her and urges flexibility, but their discussion becomes a bitter rupture. Antigone is sealed in a tomb. The prophet Tiresias then reports signs that the gods reject the city's sacrifices because Polynices is unburied and Antigone has been entombed alive. Creon reluctantly reverses himself, but too late: Antigone has hanged herself; Haemon dies by suicide after confronting his father; and Eurydice, hearing of Haemon's death, also kills herself. Creon remains alive to acknowledge that his pride and refusal to listen brought the catastrophe upon his own house.

characters.description: A daughter of Oedipus and sister of the two princes who have killed each other in the struggle for Thebes. Antigone believes the sacred obligation to bury her brother Polyneices outweighs the king's decree forbidding it. She asks Ismene to help and is prepared to act alone when her sister refuses.
characters.name: Antigone

characters.description: Antigone's sister and the other surviving daughter of Oedipus. Ismene shares her grief but fears that defying the ruler will destroy the last members of their family. She urges caution and refuses to join the planned burial.
characters.name: Ismene

characters.description: The new king of Thebes and uncle of Antigone and Ismene. After defending the city against Polyneices' attack, Creon orders honourable burial for Eteocles but leaves Polyneices unburied as a traitor. He treats obedience to civic authority as the test of loyalty.
characters.name: Creon

characters.description: Antigone's dead brother, who attacked Thebes after a dispute over the throne and died fighting his brother Eteocles. Creon's order denies his body burial, making the treatment of his remains the central conflict of the play.
characters.name: Polyneices

characters.description: The brother of Antigone, Ismene, and Polyneices. He died defending Thebes in single combat with Polyneices and receives the public honours that Creon denies his brother.
characters.name: Eteocles

characters.description: A sentry assigned to watch Polyneices' body. Frightened of Creon's temper, he reports that someone has performed burial rites despite the decree and tries to make clear that the guards did not willingly fail in their duty.
characters.name: Guard

characters.description: Creon's son and Antigone's intended husband. Haemon initially approaches his father with respect, then argues that the city sympathizes with Antigone and that a ruler should be willing to reconsider a mistaken judgment.
characters.name: Haemon

characters.description: The aged blind prophet of Thebes. Tiresias interprets signs from the gods and advises Creon that the unburied corpse and Antigone's punishment have polluted the city. His long record of truthful counsel gives the warning political as well as religious weight.
characters.name: Tiresias

characters.description: Creon's wife and Haemon's mother. She enters late to hear the report from the place where Antigone was confined and asks for a plain account of what has happened to her family.
characters.name: Eurydice

characters.description: A group of Theban elders who respond to the conflict and advise Creon. The Chorus reflects the city's relief after the failed invasion, its respect for authority, and its growing fear that the king's refusal to bend is violating divine order.
characters.name: Chorus of Theban Elders

recaps.ending: Tiresias warns that Creon's treatment of Polyneices and Antigone has offended the gods. Creon finally yields and goes first to bury Polyneices, then to release Antigone from the stone chamber. The reversal comes too late. Antigone has hanged herself. Haemon, grieving beside her, attacks his father unsuccessfully and then kills himself. When Eurydice hears that her son is dead, she withdraws into the palace and takes her own life, condemning Creon for the deaths of their children. Creon returns carrying Haemon's body and learns of his wife's death. Having lost his family through the decree he defended as necessary to the state, he recognizes his own responsibility and asks to be led away. The Chorus closes by linking wisdom with reverence for divine law and by presenting suffering as the punishment that teaches the proud.
recaps.in_short: After Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polyneices kill each other fighting over Thebes, the new king Creon honours Eteocles but forbids burial of Polyneices as a traitor. Their sister Antigone believes divine and family duties require burial and performs the rites despite the threat of death. Creon refuses appeals from Antigone, Ismene, the Theban elders, and his son Haemon, who is pledged to marry her. He orders Antigone sealed in a rocky chamber. The prophet Tiresias then warns that the gods reject Thebes' sacrifices because Creon has left a corpse exposed and entombed a living person. Creon finally reverses course, buries Polyneices, and goes to free Antigone, but she has killed herself. Haemon dies beside her, and his mother Eurydice kills herself after hearing the news. Creon survives to recognize that his rigidity destroyed his family, while the Chorus identifies humility and respect for divine law as the wisdom purchased by his suffering.

recaps.text: Thebes has survived an attack led by Polyneices, one of the sons of Oedipus. Polyneices and his brother Eteocles have killed each other, leaving their uncle Creon to rule. Antigone secretly tells her sister Ismene that Creon has ordered Eteocles buried with honour but forbidden anyone to bury Polyneices. For Antigone, the command conflicts with obligations owed to the dead and to the gods. She asks Ismene to help cover their brother's body. Ismene is afraid of the death penalty and argues that the surviving sisters have too little power to challenge the state. Antigone rejects caution, declares that she will perform the burial herself, and leaves Ismene distressed but unable to stop her.

The Chorus of Theban elders celebrates the city's escape from conquest. Creon addresses them as the new king and defines loyalty to the city as the basis of good rule. He announces that Eteocles will receive full honours while Polyneices must remain exposed, guarded against anyone attempting burial. A frightened sentry then reports that someone has scattered dust over Polyneices and carried out the minimum funeral observance without leaving a clear trace. Creon suspects bribery and conspiracy rather than religious duty. He threatens the guards unless they find the offender, turning the unexplained rite into a direct test of his authority.

The guards clear the dust and keep watch. When Antigone returns and repeats the rites, they arrest her and bring her before Creon. She admits the act without hesitation and argues that his proclamation cannot cancel older divine laws governing the dead. Creon regards her defiance, and especially her refusal to submit after being caught, as intolerable. Ismene tries to share responsibility, but Antigone will not let her claim a deed she declined to perform. Creon condemns Antigone despite her engagement to his son. Haemon approaches respectfully and urges his father to listen to the citizens, who pity Antigone, and to remain flexible. Creon interprets disagreement as disobedience. Their argument ends with Haemon leaving in anger and Creon resolved to confine Antigone alive in a stone chamber.

Antigone is led away to the chamber where she will be sealed with only a small provision of food. She mourns the marriage and ordinary life she will never have, while still holding to the duty that brought her sentence. Creon refuses to accept responsibility for her coming death because the confinement leaves her fate formally to the gods. Tiresias arrives with evidence that the city's religious rites are failing: birds and sacrificial signs have been polluted by remains taken from Polyneices' unburied body. He warns that Creon has reversed the proper order by keeping a dead man above ground and placing a living woman below it. Creon first accuses the prophet of corruption, but Tiresias predicts deaths within Creon's own household. After the prophet leaves, the shaken Chorus persuades the king to undo his commands.

Creon finally arranges burial for Polyneices and then hurries to release Antigone, but his change of mind is too late. At the chamber, Antigone has hanged herself. Haemon is beside her; after attempting to strike Creon, he turns his weapon on himself and dies holding Antigone. A messenger brings the news to Eurydice. She listens quietly, enters the palace, and kills herself, blaming Creon for the loss of her sons. Creon returns carrying Haemon's body and is told of his wife's death. The king who treated compromise as weakness is left alive without his family, acknowledging that his own decisions caused the disaster. He asks his attendants to take him away. The Chorus concludes that pride and irreverence bring severe punishment and that wisdom often arrives only through suffering.

characters.description: A fifteen-year-old boy in Lexington, Massachusetts, frustrated that his father still treats him as a child. Thoughtful, argumentative, and eager to prove himself, he measures adulthood at first by independence and recognition, just before the colonial crisis makes that question immediate and dangerous.
characters.name: Adam Cooper

characters.description: Adam's stern, principled father, a farmer and active member of the Lexington community. He expects hard work and disciplined reasoning from his sons and often answers Adam's uncertainty with criticism, though his demands are rooted in deeply held ideas about responsibility and freedom.
characters.name: Moses Cooper

characters.description: Adam and Levi's mother, who holds the Cooper household together with practical intelligence. She understands the affection beneath Adam's clashes with Moses and tries to mediate without weakening either of them.
characters.name: Sarah Cooper

characters.description: Adam's younger brother, still openly childish where Adam is desperate to appear grown. Curious and excitable, he watches Adam closely and helps reveal how recently Adam himself occupied the role he now rejects.
characters.name: Levi Cooper

characters.description: The formidable elder of the Cooper household. Blunt, experienced, and unimpressed by male solemnity, she speaks more freely than the others and offers Adam an affectionate counterweight to his father's severity.
characters.name: Granny Cooper

characters.description: The Lexington girl Adam loves. Their courtship is young and sometimes awkward, but she takes his thoughts seriously and represents a future that feels personal rather than political as the town's danger grows.
characters.name: Ruth Simmons

characters.description: Ruth's father and one of the local men drawn into Lexington's deliberations. Connected to the Coopers by family and community ties, he treats the dispute with Britain as a practical question that ordinary households can no longer avoid.
characters.name: Cousin Simmons

characters.description: Lexington's minister and an influential voice in the town. He helps frame resistance in moral as well as political terms while the community debates how to answer British pressure.
characters.name: Jonas Clarke

characters.description: An older colonial fighter whom Adam encounters after the shooting on Lexington Green. Experienced, steady, and unsentimental, he guides the exhausted boy through the improvised fighting that follows and gives him a model of courage grounded in judgment rather than display.
characters.name: Solomon Chandler

recaps.ending: After surviving the clash on Lexington Green and joining the attacks on the British column returning from Concord, Adam comes home physically exhausted and emotionally older. Moses is dead, and Adam must face Sarah, Levi, Granny, and Ruth with the knowledge that the morning's public history is also his family's private catastrophe. The community prepares its dead for burial while trying to understand that a political quarrel has become a war. Adam no longer needs the abstract recognition he wanted from his father: carrying fear, responsibility, and grief has forced adulthood upon him. At the same time, the novel does not make combat glorious. Adam's new maturity consists largely in knowing its cost and in accepting that ordinary life, family duties, and his relationship with Ruth must continue after irreversible loss.
recaps.in_short: On April 18, 1775, fifteen-year-old Adam Cooper of Lexington longs for his stern father Moses to recognize him as a man. Their household arguments unfold while the town debates resistance to British authority. Adam signs the militia muster roll, and during the night riders warn that British regulars are approaching. On Lexington Green the local militia faces the column in a confused confrontation. A shot is fired, the British volley, and Moses is killed. Adam escapes in terror, then meets the experienced Solomon Chandler and joins colonists firing on the British retreat from Concord. The day's fear and violence replace Adam's romantic ideas about courage with direct knowledge of death and responsibility. He returns to Sarah, Levi, Granny, and Ruth as the community mourns. The war has begun, Moses is gone, and Adam has acquired the adult standing he wanted in a form he never imagined and cannot celebrate.

recaps.text: Fifteen-year-old Adam Cooper lives with his parents, Moses and Sarah, his younger brother Levi, and Granny in Lexington, Massachusetts. He feels trapped between childhood and adulthood: he works like a man and thinks seriously, yet Moses corrects him sharply and rarely offers the approval he wants. Their disagreement over the meaning of a biblical passage becomes another contest over whether Adam can reason for himself. Adam finds more ease with his sharp-tongued grandmother and with Ruth Simmons, the girl he hopes to marry someday. Beyond the household, the dispute between the colonies and Britain is no longer distant. Lexington's families discuss rights, armed resistance, and the possibility that British troops may move against stores in the countryside. Adam wants a clear chance to prove his courage, but he still imagines danger as something that will settle his place in the eyes of others.

Lexington's men debate their obligations as British subjects and as members of a community that believes its liberties are being taken away. The arguments mingle principle with uncertainty: no one knows whether resistance will prevent violence or bring it closer. Adam attends the gathering and signs the militia muster roll. The act gives him the public standing he has wanted, and Moses's response carries a new recognition that his son has accepted an adult duty. Late that night, warning riders report that British regulars are marching from Boston toward Concord. Bells and messengers rouse the town. The militia gathers while families prepare for an encounter whose scale and purpose remain unclear. Adam reports with the others, excited by inclusion but increasingly conscious that the weapons and hurried farewells are real. His private struggle with his father is overtaken by the need for both of them to stand in the same line.

Before dawn on April 19, the Lexington militia assembles on the common as the British column approaches. The local men are badly outnumbered and do not intend to begin a battle, but shouted orders, movement, and confusion leave both sides tense. An unidentified shot breaks the standoff. The British soldiers fire a volley and charge. Adam experiences the event not as an orderly patriotic scene but as noise, smoke, panic, and bodies falling. Moses is shot and killed. Adam, overwhelmed by terror and unable to help his father, runs from the green. In a few moments the recognition he sought from Moses becomes meaningless beside the fact that there will be no further conversation between them. The town's political debate has become bloodshed, and Adam's first response is survival rather than the heroic conduct he had imagined.

Adam hides and struggles to master his panic after fleeing the green. Shame at running competes with shock and grief, but the scattered colonists around him make clear that fear is not unique to him. The British continue toward Concord, while armed men from surrounding towns move toward the road. Adam meets Solomon Chandler, an older and more experienced fighter who neither romanticizes danger nor dismisses the boy. Under Chandler's guidance, Adam rejoins the colonial effort. Rather than forming ranks for another open confrontation, the colonists use walls, trees, and their knowledge of the country to harass the British column. Adam fires at men he cannot know personally and begins to understand warfare as a chain of frightened human choices, not the clean test of manhood he once expected. Following Chandler gives him enough structure to act while he is still absorbing Moses's death.

The fighting intensifies as the British retreat from Concord toward Boston and more colonial militia arrive along the route. Adam remains with Solomon Chandler through exhaustion, danger, and the disorienting knowledge that his own shots may kill. By the time he returns to Lexington, the single day has stripped away his earlier desire for a dramatic proof of courage. Moses is dead, and Sarah, Levi, Granny, Ruth, and the rest of the community must absorb losses that public talk of liberty cannot soften. Adam comes home changed: he has stood with adults and acted under fire, but the recognition costs him the father from whom he wanted it. As Lexington tends its wounded and buries its dead, everyone understands that the confrontation is not an isolated disturbance but the opening of a larger war. Adam accepts new responsibilities within his family and moves toward Ruth with a more sober sense of the life they might build amid uncertainty.
